October · Week 40

Numbers & Counting 🔢

October 1 – October 7, 2027 · Days 274–280

Azlyn can recite numbers to twenty and still not know what one of them means. Every number this week lands on something she can touch, hear or stand on. Friday she builds a board game and numbers twenty squares in her own hand. Saturday she lays eight places for eight guests and finds the one that is short a spoon. Sunday the numbers arrive as coins dropping into a cookie tin with her eyes shut. Monday she runs a hall floor taped 0 to 10, Tuesday she climbs eight stairs with her voice rising a note a step, Wednesday she runs that same hall and stops dead on the number she picked herself, and by Thursday she reads four dots off a card and plays them back on a bucket.

No holiday lands this week, so October does the work: one tree with half its leaves up and half already down, sidewalk she can kick through, wet railings that ring under a stick, and the light going gold by five. Two threads run the week. On five of the seven days the counting jar comes down for one round at a time and goes back on a high shelf after, because everything in it is the size that chokes Kreston. The hall number line goes down on Monday and stays taped until Thursday afternoon, when she walks it one last time and peels it up.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • One number for one thing. Forty objects into a jar, eight plates onto a table, a finger on each as she goes. Touching every item is what stops the count drifting.
  • The numerals 0 to 10. She writes them on cards, tapes them down the hall, and runs to the one you call without counting up from the start.
  • Counting sounds she cannot see. Coins into a tin behind a dish towel, knocks through a closed door, four beats on a pan. The number has to be held in her head.
  • Stopping on a number. A tower that halts at seven with the next cup already in her hand, and a run down the hall that ends where the count says it ends.
  • Rules she invents and then has to live with. She dictates the board game rules onto a card, and they bind her the same as they bind you.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 15 months this week. He runs, spoons his own food and points at pictures in books, so name whatever his finger lands on and then say how many of them there are. He turns 16 months on Tuesday the 5th, and from that morning he stacks four blocks, copies whatever chore you are doing, and has ten words or more to work with.

🌍 Around the world Week 40 · read it on Day 274

Counting on Your Hands, Everywhere 🖐️

Hands count higher than ten across a lot of the world. In parts of India, Pakistan and Egypt people count the joints of the four fingers with the thumb, which reaches twelve on one hand. Chinese hand numbers run to ten on a single hand, a different finger shape for each.

✨
Try it

Count twelve raisins onto her plate the Indian way, thumb walking up the finger joints, three joints to a finger.

👩 What you'll learn
  • Inventing a game is a much bigger deal than playing one
  • Hosting is a social skill, and it's learnable at three
  • Predicting a sound and then testing it is her first real hypothesis
  • Loud is a developmental need, not a provocation
  • High and low is a confusing pair of words
  • Freezing on cue is genuine impulse control
  • Copying a rhythm is harder than it looks, and it's a working memory task
Did you know

Counting finger joints is where the dozen comes from. Twelve eggs in a box, twelve months in a year.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Forty Things in the Counting Jar

You need: 1 large jar or clear tub with a lid · 40 small objects (buttons, coins, dried pasta, bottle caps) · 1 tray.

  1. Tip the forty objects onto the tray and push it in front of her. She sorts before she counts, so let that run.
  2. Count ten into your hand out loud, one object per number, and drop them in the jar. She loads the other thirty.
  3. Ask how many are in there. Take her answer as it comes and tell her the jar is the bank for the game she builds at 9:15.

⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Track With Twenty Squares

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 large flattened cardboard box, 1 thick marker, 1 straight strip of card to rule the lines, The counting jar, 40 small objects, 1 paper cup as the shaker, 3 dried butter beans, one side of each colored with the marker, 1 roll masking tape, Paper and a pencil for her rules

  1. Lay the flattened box on the floor. Rule a snaking track of twenty squares across it with the marker and the card strip, each square wide enough for her hand.
  2. Hand her the marker. She numbers the squares 1 to 20 herself. Backwards fives and a 12 running off the edge all count. Write the numerals she asks for.
  3. Color one side of each butter bean. Drop all three in the paper cup, shake, tip them out and count the colored sides facing up. That is how many squares you move.
  4. She picks the counters out of the jar, a button for her and a bottle cap for you. Tape a strip across square one, write START on it, and tape another across twenty.
  5. Play one round with no rules. Somewhere in it she will announce one. Write every rule she invents on the paper with the pencil, word for word, then read the list back before the next game and play by all of it.

💡Her rules will favor her. Play them straight and lose. She is watching to see whether a rule she made holds when it costs you the game.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

How Many Steps to the Mailbox

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk to the mailbox counting your steps out loud, one number per foot, and let her count hers coming back. Count curbs and drain covers on the way home.

The Game in a Box

Getting the game to the grandparents at half past two means packing it into something she can carry.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 shoebox or cereal box with a lid, Thick card for the counters and the rules card, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), Crayons, 1 thick marker, 1 roll masking tape, The board, the paper cup, the beans and the jar counters from this morning, 1 paper bag for carrying it

  1. Count the players out loud, teddies included. Cut one counter from thick card for each of them while she calls out the shapes she wants.
  2. She colors every counter and draws a face on it. Write the name of its owner on the back in marker.
  3. Swap the card counters onto the board, tip the buttons and bottle caps back into the jar, and put the jar up on a high shelf.
  4. Fold the board in half, press the crease flat and run masking tape along it so it folds without tearing.
  5. She dictates the rules and you write them on the card in marker, one per line, with a small picture beside each so she can read them back on her own.
  6. Load the box: counters, cup, beans, rules card. The folded board goes in the paper bag with the box on top, and she writes the name of the game on the lid in crayon.
  7. Play one game out of the packed box before it goes anywhere.

💡Let her carry the bag herself. A game she made and hauled to another house is worth more than one she was handed.

Day 274 · For the grown-up Her Own Board Game · Friday, October 1
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 15 months and runs, so let him walk the last stretch on his own feet with one hand in yours. Count his steps out loud too, slow, one number per step.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Give him the shoebox lid and four card offcuts at the grandparents' feet. At 15 months he fills a container and empties it again for as long as anyone keeps handing the pieces back.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Inventing a game is a much bigger deal than playing one.

Playing a game means holding somebody else's rules in your head. Making one means deciding what the rules are, which needs her to imagine a system that does not exist yet and then hold it steady while other people act inside it. Three-year-olds who invent games run ahead on planning and on the flexible thinking that lets them change a rule once it stops working. Her rules will be unfair and they will drift mid-game, and she will hold you to them harder than she holds herself. Write them down anyway and play by them. Treating her system as real is what keeps her building systems.

⚠️

Safety: The counting jar holds buttons, coins, dried pasta and bottle tops, every one of them the size that chokes a 15-month-old who runs and still puts things in his mouth. The jar goes up high the moment counting stops, and it stays up all week. The scissors stay with you. Counting drain covers puts both of them at the curb, so hold his hand from the curb onward, keep the grating on your side of him, and walk Azlyn on the house side.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

A Chair for Every Guest

You need: 4 dining chairs · 4 cushions · her teddies.

  1. Tell her eight are coming to a party at her table today and ask who they are. Take the list as she gives it, teddies and all.
  2. Count the guests with her, one finger per name, and stop at eight however you get there.
  3. Set four chairs at the table and lay four cushions along the far edge of the table, so the smaller guests sit up at it. Count the eight seats out loud, then count the eight guests again, and leave the table bare.

Setting Eight Places

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 8 plates, 8 cups, 8 spoons, 8 napkins or squares of paper towels, 4 chairs and 4 cushions, Paper and 1 marker for the numbered place cards, 1 tray, The snack to divide: crackers, grapes quartered lengthways, sliced banana

  1. Fold eight bits of paper into standing cards and write 1 to 8 on them in marker while she watches. She adds her own marks to each one.
  2. She walks the table and puts one card at each place. Eight cards, eight guests, and she will land on seven or nine the first time.
  3. Load the tray with eight plates. She carries and lays them one per card, then comes back for the cups, the spoons and the napkins, one kind of thing per trip.
  4. Take one spoon away while she is looking elsewhere. Walk round the table touching each place and counting out loud, and let her find the place that is short.
  5. Sit the guests down. Chairs for the four who need them, cushions for the four who do not.
  6. Snack at 10:15 happens at her table. One cracker, one slice of banana and two grape quarters on every plate, counted out by her.

💡She will lose count at six and start from one again. Let her, as often as she needs.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Eight Leaves for Eight Places

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a paper bag out and bring back eight leaves, one for every place at the table. Early October is the best week of the year for it: yellow, green, brown and red on one tree. Count them into the bag and out again on the doorstep.

The Tea Party She Runs

Eight places are laid and nothing has happened at them yet. She hosts.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The set table, eight places, 1 small pitcher of water or juice she can lift with two hands, A plate of cookies and cut fruit, 1 notepad and 1 pencil for the orders, 1 dish towel, The counting jar as the register

  1. She stands at the door and lets the guests in one at a time, showing each to a numbered place. You carry the teddies and wait to be seated.
  2. She goes round with the notepad and the pencil and takes everyone's order. Her writing is a scribble per guest.
  3. Two of everything onto each plate off the serving plate, cookies and fruit, counted out loud as she goes.
  4. Pouring. Both hands on the pitcher, one cup at a time, and the dish towel is hers for what lands on the table.
  5. Set the counting jar beside her as the register. Everyone pays at the end and she counts out what she is owed, one button per guest.
  6. Goodbyes at the door, one guest at a time, counted out of the room as they leave. Eight in, eight out.
  7. Clear together. She stacks the cups in fours and tells you how many that makes.

💡Order something awkward. Ask for four cookies and no fruit and let her say no.

Day 275 · For the grown-up Eight Places at the Table · Saturday, October 2
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 15 months and spoons his own food, so give him a real place at the table with a plate and a spoon rather than a tray on the floor. His come out of the cupboard and sit outside her count, because the eight are hers. Outside, let him carry one leaf the whole way home in his fist.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Carry him for the first room at the museum and put him down in the second. At 15 months he points at pictures, so watch where his finger goes and name whatever it lands on.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Hosting is a social skill, and it's learnable at three.

Greeting somebody, seating them, asking what they want and handing it over in the right order is a long chain of steps held together by attention to another person. Azlyn has spent three years on the receiving end of it, and running the party herself flips her into the role that has to track what everyone else needs. That tracking is perspective-taking, the thing that makes sharing and turn-taking possible later. She will forget a guest and pour for herself first. The sequence is what she is learning, and she gets it from doing the job rather than from being reminded to be polite.

⚠️

Safety: Party food ends up on the floor and Kreston is down there at speed. Grapes quartered lengthways, no whole nuts, nothing hot within reach of either child, and a sweep between the party and the crawling. The counting jar goes back up high the moment the register closes.

🌅 START
Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

One at a Time Into the Tin

You need: 1 empty metal cookie tin · 10 coins or smooth pebbles.

  1. Drop one coin into the empty tin from a hand's height. Then two, one after the other, a beat apart, and say the number each time it lands.
  2. Hand her the coins. She drops, you count out loud, and the two of you find the speed where the numbers still fit between the sounds.
  3. Tip the tin out and count them back in together. Tell her that at 9:15 she does the same job with her eyes shut.
Materials, laid out d276-materials.png

Day 276 · The main event Counting With Her Ears · Sunday, October 3
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

How Many Did You Hear

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 metal cookie tin or saucepan, 10 coins or smooth pebbles, A handful of dried pasta, 1 dish towel to hide the drops, The counting jar, 1 wooden spoon

  1. Sit facing each other across the table with the tin between you and the dish towel draped over your dropping hand.
  2. She shuts her eyes. Drop between one and five coins, one at a time with a clear gap, and let her say the number before she opens them.
  3. Count them out of the tin together to check. She will be right on two and three long before she is right on five.
  4. Swap over. She drops, you guess, and you get one wrong on purpose to see what she does with that.
  5. Change the sound. Dried pasta lands soft, a pebble lands hard, and the wooden spoon on the tin rim is louder than either. Ask her which is easiest to count and take her answer.
  6. Refill from the counting jar when the coins run short, and put the jar back up high when you finish.

💡Leave a full second between drops. Two sounds that arrive together are one sound to her, and the gap is what turns a noise into a number.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

One Finger for Every Sound

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk to a bench, sit down and shut your eyes for a slow count of ten. One finger goes up for every separate sound: a car, a dog, a plane, feet on wet leaves. Compare hands at the end. October Sunday mornings are quiet enough for this to work and cold enough that you both want to move again after.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Knock Three Times, Bring Me Three

A number she cannot see has to be held in her head long enough to act on it. The knocking is the order and the basket is the answer.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: A door or the table to knock on, 1 wooden spoon, 1 basket, The counting jar, Paper and 1 crayon for the tally

  1. Knock three times on the table, slow. She fetches three things from the room and puts them in the basket, whatever they turn out to be.
  2. Count them out together. Draw three marks on the paper with the crayon and write 3 at the end of the row.
  3. Go up and down between one and five. Empty the basket after each round so she starts from nothing.
  4. Move out of sight and knock on the door instead. She has to count with nothing to look at, which is the version she finds hard.
  5. Swap over. She knocks with the wooden spoon and sends you off, and you come back with the wrong number twice so she gets to correct you.
  6. Counting jar round: she counts that many buttons out of the jar into the basket, then tips them back and the jar goes up high.
  7. Finish on a big one. Knock eight times and watch her carry what she can and come back for the rest.

💡She will start moving before you have finished knocking. Say the count out loud with the last few knocks for a round or two, then drop your voice again.

Day 276 · For the grown-up Counting With Her Ears · Sunday, October 3
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 15 months and points at whatever he notices. Sit him on the bench between you and watch where his finger goes when a plane crosses over. Name it, then say how many, and he gets the count attached to the thing he already found.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take the basket out with you. At 15 months he carries a thing while he runs and hands it over when somebody puts a hand out, so let him load one leaf at a time into the basket at the playground. Buckeyes stay in your pocket. Count the leaves onto the doorstep with him when you get home.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Predicting a sound and then testing it is her first real hypothesis.

Azlyn hears four drops, says four, opens her eyes and counts four coins in the tin. She has made a claim, checked it against the world and found out she was right, which is the shape of every experiment she will ever run. Guessing from sound alone forces her to hold a count in her head without the steadying help of fingers or objects, and that mental version arrives later than the pointing kind. Being wrong matters as much as being right here. The tin hands her the answer without anybody having to tell her, and a wrong guess sends her straight back in for another round.

⚠️

Safety: Coins, pebbles, dried pasta and buttons are every one of them the size that chokes a 15-month-old, and Kreston runs. Sweep the floor between rounds, count the coins back into the tin before he goes down, and the counting jar goes up high the moment the round ends.

🌅 START
Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Five Buckets, Biggest to Smallest

You need: 5 buckets, tins or saucepans in different sizes · 1 wooden spoon.

  1. Line the five up across the floor, biggest to smallest, and let her move any she disagrees with.
  2. Tap each one twice with the spoon, working down the line. The big ones boom and the small ones ring, and she will hear the order change.
  3. Ask her which one is the loudest and let her prove it. That one goes on the end and it is number five at 9:15.

Day 277 · The main event Loud Numbers · Monday, October 4
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Five Is the Loudest

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 5 buckets, tins or saucepans in different sizes, 2 wooden spoons, 1 roll masking tape, 1 thick marker, 1 sheet of card folded into a 1-to-5 dial, 1 cushion for Kreston, well back

  1. Put Kreston on his cushion at the far end of the room, a good distance back, before anything gets hit.
  2. Stick a strip of masking tape on each bucket and number them 1 to 5 in marker, quietest to loudest, in the order she settled on at breakfast.
  3. Fold the card into five panels and write a big numeral on each. That is the dial, and she holds it.
  4. She shows a number and everyone plays eight beats at that volume. Count the eight out loud together, spoons on the buckets, and stop dead on eight.
  5. She changes the number between rounds. One is a fingertip on the rim, five is both spoons on the big bucket, and she calls which arrives.
  6. Count down to finish. Five, four, three, two, one, then zero, and zero is silence held for a slow count of five with the spoons on the floor.

💡Give her the dial and keep your hands on a bucket. A three-year-old told all week to keep it down plays the quiet numbers with care once the loud ones are hers to call.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Loud Twenty, Quiet Twenty

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Find a path with nobody's window on it and count twenty steps at the top of your voices, then twenty more in a whisper. October wind takes the loud numbers off across the field, and the quiet ones make her lean in to hear yours.

Zero to Ten Down the Hallway

The hall floor becomes a number line this afternoon, and it stays down until Thursday.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 roll masking tape, 1 thick marker, 11 pieces of paper numbered 0 to 10, 1 sock ball or beanbag, A clear stretch of hall floor

  1. Write 0 to 10 on the eleven sheets in marker, one numeral per sheet, and let her do the ones she can.
  2. Tape them down the hall, a stride apart, 0 at the near end and 10 at the far one. She lays them, you tape.
  3. Walk the line together saying each number as a foot lands on it. Then back the other way, 10 down to 0.
  4. Call a number and she runs to it. Call another before she has stopped. Six or seven rounds and she stops looking at 0 to work out where 7 is.
  5. Throw the sock ball down the line. She fetches it, names the number it landed on and counts her steps back to you.
  6. Stand her on 3 and ask for two steps forward. Ask where she is now.
  7. Leave the whole thing taped down. She will walk it on her own at 4:15 and you need it again on Wednesday and Thursday.

💡Zero earns its own sheet.

The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 40Day 277 · afternoon →
Finished result d277-result.png
✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • Line up to five only, and jump it.
  • Chalk the same line outside if the hall is impossible.
  • Lay the numbers out of order and let her sort them.
  • Hop it on one foot, then walk it backwards.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The hill walk, counting the stops on the way up
  • The neighborhood park, and the long way round
  • A field walk in rain boots, because the ground has turned
  • The playground with the big slide
Day 277 · For the grown-up Loud Numbers · Monday, October 4
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 15 months and runs, so let him do the loud twenty on his own feet between you. Watch his face on the quiet twenty: dropping to a whisper makes most 15-month-olds copy the volume before they copy the words.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He will be on the number line the second it is down. At 15 months he walks a taped path for the pleasure of the line under his feet, and the numbers mean nothing to him yet. Say them anyway as he passes each sheet. Tape the corners flat so nobody skids on a loose one.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Loud is a developmental need, not a provocation.

Banging a saucepan is how Azlyn finds out what her arms can do to the world. She is calibrating force against result, and loud is the end of the scale that gives the clearest reading. Volume also carries feeling before words can, so a morning of noise she is allowed to make drains off what would come out later as a floor tantrum. Handing her the dial changes what the noise is for: she has to hold a number, watch other people follow it, and cut the sound off on eight. You get the loud out on purpose, at a time you chose, and the quiet numbers come easier all week.

⚠️

Safety: Close-range banging is loud enough to damage a 15-month-old's hearing. Keep Kreston a room's width from the buckets, work in short bursts with quiet gaps, and stop the moment he startles, covers his ears or turns away. Never let the spoons swing near his head.

One Cup, Two Cups, Eight Cups

You need: 8 jam jars on a tray · 1 pitcher of water · 1 small cup for pouring.

  1. Count the jars along the tray with her, left to right, and let her tell you which one she thinks will end up heaviest.
  2. She pours eight cupfuls into jar one and seven into jar two, counting each pour out loud as it goes in. The row empties out as it goes along.
  3. Stop there and leave the other six. Ask her what she thinks jar eight will look like when it only gets one, and tell her she fills the rest at 9:15.

Eight Jars and a Spoon

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 8 jam jars or glass tumblers, all the same size, 1 metal teaspoon, 1 pitcher of water, 1 small cup for pouring, Food coloring, 1 drop per jar (optional), 1 tray, Masking tape and 1 marker for the numbers

  1. Tape a strip in front of each jar and number them 1 to 8 in marker. She fills jars three to eight, counting the cupfuls down the row: six cups into jar three, five into jar four, on down to one cup into jar eight.
  2. Top the pitcher up as she goes. Spills land on the tray.
  3. One drop of food coloring in each jar if you have it. She stirs with the teaspoon and eight jars of water become eight different things.
  4. Tap each jar on the rim with the teaspoon, working from one to eight, and let the line of sounds land before anyone says a word.
  5. Ask which jar holds the most water and which made the deepest sound, then check her answer by tapping those two again.
  6. She plays the whole ladder, one to eight and back down to one, counting as she taps.

💡Say deep and thin rather than low and high for the first half hour.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Leaves Still Up, Leaves Already Down

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Stand under one tree and count ten leaves still up in the branches, then ten already down at your feet. First week of October and most trees are half and half, so one tree gives you both. Point up on the counting up and crouch on the counting down.

Up the Stairs, One Note at a Time

The jars gave her a ladder she could hear. The stairs give her one she can climb.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: The stairs, or a chair, the sofa and the floor as three heights, Masking tape and 1 marker for numbering the steps, The jars from this morning, left on their tray on the table as the reference, 1 metal teaspoon, The stair gate, shut

  1. Tape a numbered strip on the first eight stairs, 1 at the bottom. Shut the stair gate at the bottom with Kreston on the far side of it, and keep to one person on the stairs at a time.
  2. She sits on stair one and sings a low note. Up to stair two, and her voice goes up with her. Follow her rather than lead.
  3. Climb to eight, a note a stair, then come back down and let the voice drop with each step.
  4. Leave the jars on the table and go back to them between climbs. Tap jar one with the teaspoon, then jar eight, and ask her which stair each one belongs on. The full deep one lives at the bottom.
  5. Call a number. She climbs to that stair and sings the note she thinks lives there.
  6. Swap. She calls the number, you climb, and you go to the wrong stair once so she can send you back.
  7. Take the tape off the stairs before dinner. Tape underfoot on a staircase is a fall waiting to happen.

💡The floor, the sofa and a chair make three heights if the stairs are out.

  • Sing the numbers up and down without the stairs at all.
  • Pour the jars back into the pitcher, counting the cupfuls out.
  • Tap the jars while she hides her eyes and guesses high or low.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • Swimming, and count the steps into the water
  • The library, if the pool is booked out for lessons
  • Indoor playground, counting the steps up to the slide
  • A short walk while the light lasts, which is going fast now
Day 278 · For the grown-up High Notes, Low Notes · Tuesday, October 5
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston turns 16 months today. Say it out loud, because nobody else will. He stacks four blocks now and copies whatever a grown-up is doing, so hand him a leaf and hold your own up high.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He comes to the pool at 16 months and copies everything you do in the water. Hold his hands and count three, two, one before every lift and dip. Twenty minutes and out. October cold arrives fast and he will not say so until he shivers.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

High and low is a confusing pair of words.

Azlyn already uses high and low for where a thing sits on a shelf. Asking her to hear a high note means bolting a second meaning onto a word she has settled, and three-year-olds sort this out by lining the two up rather than by being told they are different. Climbing a stair while her voice rises gives her height, number and pitch moving together in one action, and the match does the teaching. Reaching for the top of her range while standing on the top stair is worth more than any explanation. Children whose parents sing with them hear the difference between two notes better, without a single lesson.

⚠️

Safety: Glass jars and a hard floor, and stairs with a 16-month-old who climbs. The jars stay on the tray on the table, never on the floor and never at the top of the stairs. The stair gate stays shut and one person is on the stairs at a time. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

The Number That Means Freeze

You need: 11 blank cards · 1 thick marker · masking tape.

  1. Write 0 to 10 on the cards, one numeral each, and let her take over on the ones she knows. These are the number cards for the rest of the week.
  2. Spread all eleven face up on the table and ask her to choose the one that means stop. She will pick a big one.
  3. Tape her choice to the door at her eye height. That number is the rule now, and everyone in the house has to obey it at 9:15.
Materials, laid out d279-materials.png
The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 40Day 279 · morning →
Day 279 · The main event Stop on Seven · Wednesday, October 6
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Number on the Door

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: The taped number line from Monday, still down the hall, The number cards 0 to 10, 1 roll masking tape, 1 wooden spoon and 1 pan, or music on your phone, A clear floor

  1. Read the card on the door out loud together. Say it back and forth until she can tell you what happens when the count reaches it.
  2. Bang the pan with the spoon and count up from one, slow and even, while she runs the hall from 0 to 10 and back.
  3. On her number she freezes. Keep banging past it. The count is the cue, so the noise carrying on is what makes the number do the work.
  4. Praise the stop, not the running. Hold the freeze for a slow three before you start the next count.
  5. New card every round. She takes one off the table and tapes it up herself, and low numbers come round fast.
  6. Swap over. She counts and bangs, you run the hall, and you miss the stop once so she gets to call you out.

💡Count slower than feels sensible. The gap between nine and ten is where she does the work of getting ready to stop, and a fast count takes that away.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Stopping at Every Third Tree

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the road counting trees or lampposts out loud, and stop dead at every third one. Both of you, hands in the air, until she says go. October has the sidewalk covered, so count the piles she can kick through on the way as well. Turn round at the fifteenth and count them back down to one.

Outdoors d279-outside.png

The Tower That Stops Where She Says

She sits down for this one, and the rule comes with her. Stopping a hand mid-air is harder than stopping two feet.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: 10 plastic cups or clean tins, The counting jar, The number cards 0 to 10, Paper and crayons for her stop cards, 4 blocks or small boxes for Kreston

  1. Line the ten cups up beside her and put Kreston's four blocks down at the far end of the rug. She picks a card and props it against the pile.
  2. She stacks one cup at a time, counting each one, and stops dead on her number with the next cup already in her hand.
  3. Hold it there. Count a slow three with the cup in the air, then let her carry on to ten.
  4. Bring the counting jar down to the table for one round. She drops buttons into a cup one at a time and stops on her number, then tips them back and the jar goes up high again.
  5. Paper and crayons out. She makes her own stop cards, a numeral and a picture on each, and they can be any numbers she likes.
  6. She hands you a stop card and you do the stacking. She calls the freeze, and you keep going one cup past it so she has to stop you.
  7. Last tower goes to ten with no stop at all, and she knocks it down.

💡She will fly past her number on the first two goes. Stopping wins over accuracy today, so let a tower stop on eight when the card says seven and count the stop as the win.

Day 279 · For the grown-up Stop on Seven · Wednesday, October 6
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies whatever the rest of you are doing, so he will throw his hands up a beat after Azlyn does and keep walking. That gap is real. Stopping on a signal comes later than copying the shape of it, and he is working on the shape.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Give him the four blocks on the floor beside her cups. At 16 months he stacks four and knocks them down himself, which is his whole version of this afternoon. Count his up out loud as he goes, one, two, three, four, and he will hand you the fourth one to place.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Freezing on cue is genuine impulse control.

Stopping a body that is already running takes more from Azlyn than starting one. She has to hold the rule in mind, track the count while she moves and override what her legs are doing, which are the three parts of what researchers call executive function. Games with a stop signal are one of the few things shown to move it. Tying the stop to a number rather than to the music cutting out makes it harder, because she cannot wait for silence to tell her. She has to keep her own count. Three-year-olds who play games like this get better at the stopping, and it shows up at bath time.

⚠️

Safety: Kreston stays out of the hall and at the far end of the room from the pan whichever of you is running it, because a body at full speed in a corridor does not stop for a 16-month-old. Sit him where you can see him from the hall, or use the music on your phone instead of the banging. Buttons are the size that chokes a 16-month-old. The jar round happens at the table with Kreston out of reach, the buttons are counted back in before he is on the rug again, and the jar goes up high after. Use tins for the tower only if the rims are smooth.

🌅 START
Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Two Claps, Then Wait

You need: your hands · her hands · a floor to sit on.

  1. Sit facing each other and clap twice. Wait. She claps twice back, and neither of you says anything about what the game is.
  2. Three claps, then four. Count them out loud as you go so the number arrives with the sound.
  3. Four claps with a gap in the middle. She will send back four in a row and lose the gap.
Materials, laid out d280-materials.png
The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 40Day 280 · morning →
Day 280 · The main event Clap It Back · Thursday, October 7
⏱️ 9:15 onward
🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

Four Beats, Then Your Turn

⏱️ 60 min🧰 4 items

You need: 2 wooden spoons, 1 saucepan and the buckets from Monday, Hands, knees and the floor, The counting jar, for counting out the beats

  1. Sit on the floor with the pan and the buckets between you and a spoon each.
  2. Play four even beats on the pan, counting them out loud. She plays four back. Do it until it bores her, which takes about six goes.
  3. Take the counting out. Play four beats in silence and let her count them in her head before she answers.
  4. Lay one button from the counting jar on the floor for each beat as you play it, and leave a space where a beat is missing. She reads the row and plays it. The jar goes back up high when this round ends.
  5. Move the same four beats around: hands, knees, floor, pan, bucket. The pattern stays the same and the sound changes.
  6. She leads now. She plays, you copy, and you get one wrong on purpose so she has to fix you.

💡Keep patterns to four beats today. Five is where a three-year-old drops the last one and hands back three, looking at you as though you changed it.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Railings and the Stick

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Find a stretch of railings and run a stick along them, counting the clicks. Slow first, then fast enough that neither of you can keep up with the number. Wet October railings ring where dry ones clack, and the same stick on a wooden fence goes dull. Try both and let her tell you which one she likes.

Outdoors d280-outside.png

Four Dots and a Gap

A rhythm disappears the second it stops. This afternoon hers goes onto a card and stays there.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 6 cards cut from a cereal box, 1 thick marker, Crayons, 6 clothespins and 1 length of string, The spoons and the buckets, 1 metal teaspoon, The jars from Tuesday and the hall number line, still up

  1. She plays four beats. Draw them on a card in marker as she plays, a dot for a beat and a gap for a silence.
  2. Hand her the card and ask her to play what is on it. Point at each dot as she hits it so her eye travels along the row.
  3. Six cards, six patterns, three hers and three yours, with a gap at the front of one.
  4. She colors the cards with crayons. Every dot she colors is one she has to look at.
  5. Tie the string between the front legs of two dining chairs, down at her knee height, tight enough to hold the cards. She pegs them along it in the order she picks, a peg to a card.
  6. Play the whole row left to right, spoons on the buckets, counting the dots on each card as you reach it.
  7. Finish the week: tap Tuesday's jars from one to eight with the metal teaspoon, walk the hall number line from 0 to 10, then play the card row once more. Take the string down and put it away, then peel the number line up off the hall floor with her, 10 back down to 0.

💡Read the cards left to right every time and move your finger as you go.

🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The pharmacy and the park bench, and she counts the change into your hand
  • The bakery, counting rolls into the bag
  • The park, for the leaf pile and a long run about
  • Indoor playground if the rain has set in
Day 280 · For the grown-up Clap It Back · Thursday, October 7
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so give him his own short stick and let him drag it along the low part of the railings. Say the numbers over his clicks. At 16 months he has ten words and picks up new ones attached to something he is doing.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Sit him on the bench between you at the park with the paper bag from the pharmacy. At 16 months he copies chores, so let him hand things over one at a time and thank him for each. He carries this morning's stick the whole way there and back.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Copying a rhythm is harder than it looks, and it's a working memory task.

Azlyn has to hold four beats and their spacing in her head while she waits, then get her hands to reproduce something that has already stopped existing. The four beats have to survive the gap between your hand stopping and hers starting. Nothing is left in front of her to check against. That is auditory working memory, and it sits underneath following instructions, remembering a request from the hallway and later on sounding out a word. Children who copy a rhythm well at three tend to read more easily later. Leading it is harder again, because she has to invent a pattern and hold it steady while she watches you get it wrong.

⚠️

Safety: The card line runs low between two chair legs, pulled tight and never left slack or in a loop, so there is nothing at either child's neck height. Kreston stays off that stretch of floor the whole time it is up. Take it down and put it away the moment the cards come off, because a length of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk. Buttons go on the floor only while the two of you are sitting over them, and they are back in the jar and up high before Kreston is down.

Day 281
The Car She Wears
The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 40Day 280 · for the grown-up
October · Week 41

Things That Go 🚂

October 8 – October 14, 2027 · Days 281–287

Seven days of things that move, and of what makes them move. Azlyn wears a car on Friday, races a numbered fleet down the stairs on Saturday, and spends Sunday finding out that one toy car travels four different distances on four different floors. Monday she hauls the washing the length of the hall. By Thursday the whole house has a single taped road running through it, and every build from the week sits somewhere along it.

Monday is Indigenous Peoples' Day and the afternoon walk goes along the river. One sentence about who lived along that water first is the whole treatment. This week also asks less of her than the last few weeks have, on purpose. The light goes early now, and Thursday joins up what she has already built instead of starting anything new.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Predict, then check. She calls the winner out loud before she lets go, and the tape tab on the floor settles it.
  • The floor does half the work. Six cans dragged on a blanket over carpet, then over bare boards, then the same six in a basket, and the difference arrives through her own arms.
  • Surfaces change how far things travel. Towel, cardboard, carpet, ice: one car, one ramp, four distances.
  • Drawing what is in front of her. She draws the same vehicle from memory and then from life, and says what is missing from the first one.
  • Numbers doing a job. Numbered cars, numbered parking bays, prices in bottle caps, counted back into the jar at the end.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 16 months this week. He stacks four blocks, copies whatever chore he sees you doing, and has ten words or so, which is enough to give him a real job in the middle of every activity Azlyn is running.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 41 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 41 · read it on Day 281

Vehicles Everywhere 🚐

Manila runs on jeepneys, long painted buses built out of old army jeeps and decorated by their drivers. Bangkok has the tuk-tuk, three wheels and no doors. Venice has no cars at all, so its buses float: the vaporetto pulls in at the end of the street the way a bus pulls into a curb.

✨
Try it

Serve snack off a cart. Load a tray with banana slices and crackers, park it in the hall, and let Azlyn sell to whoever walks past, the way a Manila cart does.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 41 · around the world →
Around the world w41-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • Rehearsal teaches something a spontaneous performance can't
  • A rehearsed thing needs a witness before it is finished
  • Ice is one of the few materials that changes while she's using it
  • Heavy pulling settles her faster than any conversation about the noise does
  • A darkened room helps more than a quiet one
  • Close looking is the one thing a tired child can still do
  • Mid-autumn is a low-energy stretch, and lowering the bar is the right response
Did you know

No two jeepneys are painted the same. Drivers name them and paint the name across the front.

Marking Where the Wheels Go

You need: the big box · 1 permanent marker · 5 paper plates.

  1. Stand the box up and let her climb into it, which she will do first anyway.
  2. Hold a paper plate flat against the outside while she draws round it with the marker. Four wheels, in the places she picks, even if one ends up near the roof.
  3. The fifth plate is the steering wheel. She marks its spot on the inside front and chooses where the horn goes.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Car With No Floor

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 large cardboard box, deep enough to reach her waist, 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only), 2 lengths of ribbon or string, about 2 feet each, 4 paper plates for the wheels, 1 more for the steering wheel, 1 roll masking tape, 1 permanent marker, Crayons or washable poster paint, 1 saucepan lid or a bicycle bell for the horn

  1. Cut the base clean out of the box and take the top flaps off, leaving a deep ring she can stand inside. She stands back while you cut, and you tell her why.
  2. Punch two holes in the front edge and two in the back with the point of the knife. Thread a ribbon through each pair, knot it, and tape over the knots inside.
  3. Get her into it. Shorten the ribbons until the box hangs at her waist with her arms free, then tape the slack down.
  4. Tape the four wheels onto her marks and the fifth plate inside the front as the steering wheel.
  5. Hand her the crayons or the paint. Headlights, doors, her name across the back in marker, whatever belongs on it.
  6. Tape the saucepan lid inside beside the steering wheel, or clip the bell onto the front edge.

💡Cut the base out before you cut anything else. She climbed into it at eight o'clock; with the bottom gone she wears it instead.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The First Drive Through the Leaves

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the car onto the wide flat park path and drive it through the leaves the wind brought down. She cannot see her feet in that box, so a drift arrives as sound and drag. Sweep a heap together and let her run through it.

Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Three Runs Before the Show

The car has nowhere to go yet, and tomorrow somebody sits down to watch it drive.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: The box car, 1 roll masking tape, 6 sheets of paper, 1 permanent marker, 3–4 cushions for the tunnel and the bridge, The saucepan lid horn, taped in this morning, Your phone, to film one run

  1. Tape two parallel lines down the hall to make the road, round the sofa and back to where it started. She picks the route, you tape it.
  2. Lay two cushions flat across the road as the bridge, and stand two more on end with a gap between them as the tunnel.
  3. Six sheets of paper, six signs. She draws each one, you write the word she dictates underneath, and she tapes them along the road at her height.
  4. Run one, start to finish, horn at every sign. Correct nothing.
  5. Ask her what she wants different. Change that one thing, then run it again.
  6. Run three is the filmed one. Hold the phone still and let her drive past you.
  7. Leave the road taped down overnight. It is there in the morning.

💡Three runs is the number. Two and she has not settled in, four and she is bored of her own route.

  • Strap a doll in as the passenger and drive her about.
  • Deliver something real on every run: a fork, a sock, a letter.
  • Park the box car and lay the road out for the toy vehicles.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • A friend's house, and the car travels in the trunk
  • The park path, wide and flat and empty on a Friday
  • A café with a window onto the road, counting what passes
  • The street where the trash goes out, timed for the garbage truck
Day 281 · For the grown-up The Car She Wears · Friday, October 8
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies a bigger person, so he will want a car the minute hers goes on. Tape a paper plate to each side of a shoebox and give it to him. He pushes it, loses it under the sofa, comes back for it.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 16 months he has ten words, and this afternoon hands him three: car, beep, gone. Say them as they happen instead of asking him to say them back. Let him thump the saucepan lid once, then take the car off him before he works out that it goes over a head.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Rehearsal teaches something a spontaneous performance can't.

Azlyn drove the same road three times this afternoon and changed one thing in the middle of it. That middle run is where the work sits. A child who repeats a sequence starts to hold the whole shape of it in her head instead of the next step alone, and that frees her up to notice what she wants different. Rehearsal also separates the doing from the being watched, so she gets to be bad at it in private first. By tomorrow the route costs her nothing to drive, which leaves all of her available for the person in the chair.

⚠️

Safety: The craft knife is adult-only and goes back onto a high shelf between cuts, not onto the arm of the sofa. A worn box hides her feet and puts her weight off center, so she goes over without ever seeing what caught her. No stairs and no steps in the car, and keep a hand on her anywhere near the curb.

The Fleet on the Starting Line

You need: every toy vehicle in the house · 1 roll masking tape · 1 permanent marker.

  1. Tip the lot out at the bottom of the stairs and let her line them up however she likes.
  2. Tear a tab of tape for each one, write a number on it, stick it on the roof. She says which car gets which number.
  3. Ask her which number wins. Write her answer on a tab and stick it on the wall.

The Ramp Down the Stairs

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 2–3 large boxes, flattened, Packing tape, 1 roll masking tape, 1 permanent marker, The numbered fleet, 2 heavy books, Your phone, for the finish-line photo

  1. Join the flattened boxes into one sheet with the packing tape, seams underneath.
  2. Lay it over the bottom three or four treads and weight the top edge with the two heavy books.
  3. A strip of masking tape across the top is the start line. Nothing gets a push.
  4. Release the cars one at a time. Where each stops, stick down a tab of masking tape with its number on it in marker.
  5. Crouch at the foot of the ramp, off the cardboard, and look along the spread with her. Ask her which went furthest and whether it matches the number on the wall.
  6. Photograph the floor with the tabs in shot, then let her run it again with the three she liked best.

💡She will shove them, which makes her arm the experiment instead of the car. Hold it on the line, count to three, lift your finger. She copies the count.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Acorns Down the Slide

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Fill a pocket with acorns under the oaks and take them to the slide. Send them down two at a time and call the winner before they land. Acorns roll, buckeyes roll faster, and a flat leaf goes nowhere at all. Sweep the slide clear when you leave so nobody sits on a handful.

The Grandstand Made of One Chair

One chair turns the stairs into a race meeting, and the person in it is the whole crowd.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 chair, The stair ramp and the numbered fleet, 1 roll masking tape, 3 sheets of paper and 1 marker, The box car and the saucepan lid horn, A propped-up phone, if the guest is a video call

  1. Set the chair beside the ramp, out of the run-out, with one person in it. A grandparent on a propped-up phone counts.
  2. Tickets first. She folds a sheet of paper, draws a car on it, and hands it over at the door.
  3. Re-lay the start line with masking tape and set the ramp up as it stood this morning.
  4. She announces each car by its number before she lets it go. Give her the words once (car number three, on the line), then stop feeding them.
  5. Write the finishing order on the remaining paper with the marker as she calls it out.
  6. The audience of one claps every car, including the ones that stall halfway. Say so before the first race.
  7. Last event is her lap in the box car, down the hall and back, horn past the chair.

💡Leave the chair where it is. The ramp is up by then, so at 4:15 she runs the fleet along the floor and into the shoebox past the empty chair, and that showing is hers.

  • Two cars only, best of five, and stop.
  • Build a garage at the foot of the ramp for the finishers.
  • Line the fleet up by size, then color, then speed.
  • Draw the race and post it to whoever could not come.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The fire station, or a field edge where the tractors are lifting the last of the crop
  • The garage forecourt from a safe distance, watching the lifts and the air line
  • The park, for the slide with the acorns still in her pocket
  • A bus ride to the end of the route and back, in the front seats right behind the driver
Day 282 · For the grown-up Race Day · Saturday, October 9
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and stacks four blocks now, so he builds as well as flattens. Give him four cars of his own at the far end of the room, well clear of the run-out, and let him pile them into a heap he can knock over. At the park he takes the short toddler slide on his own, sitting up and feet first, with you standing at the bottom to catch him, and never on your lap. The acorns stay in your pocket and he sends a leaf down instead.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 16 months and copies chores, so give him a real one out of the house: his own small bag to carry in and out. Back home he sits on a knee in the grandstand chair for two races. He claps when the clapping starts, a beat late and with his whole arms.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A rehearsed thing needs a witness before it is finished.

Azlyn drove her road three times yesterday for nobody, and this morning she has been waiting for the chair to be filled. Rehearsal gets the thing built; a witness closes it. Children this age treat an audience as part of the work rather than a reward at the end of it, which is why she keeps checking your face mid-race and why the same fleet run alone on the floor has a different feel for her. One person facing her, doing nothing else, does the whole job. A crowd of six splits into six half-attentions and she can feel it. A grandparent on a propped-up phone counts, which is worth knowing on a Saturday when nobody can come round.

⚠️

Safety: Cardboard taped over stair treads is a slip hazard for everybody in the house. It comes up the moment you stop racing, and nobody uses those stairs while it is down. The box-car lap stays in the hall, and the cardboard comes off the treads before she puts the car on. Hard vehicles leave the foot of the ramp fast, at Kreston's head height when he is sitting, so keep him off to the side or behind a door.

Three Roads and One in the Freezer

You need: 1 bath towel · 1 piece of flattened cardboard · a bare patch of carpet · 1 toy car.

  1. Lay the towel and the cardboard side by side on the carpet. Three roads, running next to each other.
  2. She pushes the car across each one and tells you which is fastest. Take her answer without arguing it.
  3. Tell her there is a fourth road in the freezer and keep the door shut.

Four Surfaces, One Car

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 baking tray of water, frozen overnight, 1 bath towel, 1 piece of flattened cardboard, 1 sheet of stiff card, 2 books to prop it, 1 roll masking tape, 1 permanent marker, 1 toy car, 2 old towels for the melt

  1. Prop the stiff card on the two books and tape the bottom edge down so the slope holds all morning.
  2. Lay the bath towel at the foot of the ramp and send the car down. Tab where it stops with masking tape, marked TOWEL in permanent marker.
  3. Swap in the cardboard, run it, tab it CARD. Then bare carpet, run it, tab it CARPET.
  4. Bring the ice tray out, set it at the foot of the ramp on the two old towels, and run the car onto it. It overshoots every other tab in the room, so tab that one ICE.
  5. Walk the four tabs with her and let her say which road won. She will want the ice again, so let her.
  6. Leave the ice out under her hands and run the car every ten minutes. As it goes soft the distance walks back towards the carpet tab.

💡Narrate rather than quiz. The ice is going soft, look how short that one was hands her the words while she works.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Two Sticks Off the Bridge

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take two sticks each to whatever bridge you can walk to, drop them off the upstream side together, and run to the other rail to see whose arrives first. October water runs quick and full of leaves, so half of them snag. Pick sticks of different sizes and let her call the winner before the drop.

The Parking Garage Made of Shoeboxes

Every car in the house gets a numbered bay this afternoon, in a building that comes out of the recycling.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 4–6 shoeboxes or cereal boxes, Flattened cardboard for the ramps, 1 roll masking tape, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), 1 permanent marker, 1 ruler or a straight strip of card, The fleet

  1. Lay the shoeboxes on their sides with the open ends out, two on the bottom row and the rest stacked above. Tape each joint as you go.
  2. Cut the first ramp from the flattened cardboard with the scissors while she holds the tower steady.
  3. Tape it from the floor below to the lip above and test it with one car. Cut the next only once that one runs.
  4. Rule the bays. Hold the ruler across each floor and let her draw the lines with the marker, counting as they appear.
  5. Number every bay. She calls the numbers, you write them, and the ones that come out backwards stay backwards.
  6. Park the whole fleet, one car per bay. Anything left over lines up on the ramp.
  7. Take one car off the bottom row and let her drive it up and out through every floor.

💡Build the bottom row wide. Two boxes under one carries the whole afternoon, and she will lean on it.

Day 283 · For the grown-up The Ice Road · Sunday, October 10
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies whatever he sees done, so he wants a stick the second one goes over. Hand him his own, keep a fist in the back of his coat at the rail, and let him watch it drop. In and gone are two of his ten words, and this is what they look like.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He stacks four blocks at 16 months, so give him two spare shoeboxes of his own at the other end of the table. He builds up, knocks it down, builds up again. Keep the fleet out of his half; he will put a car in his mouth inside a minute.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Ice is one of the few materials that changes while she's using it.

Most of what Azlyn plays with sits still and waits. Ice does not. It is slippery, then wet, then a puddle with a lump in it, and the change runs on a clock she can feel inside one activity. That hands her something few toys do: a before and an after she caused part of, with her own warm hands in the middle of it. Children hold on to sequences they have watched the whole way through. Say the stages out loud as they pass and the vocabulary of change (melting, softer, gone) arrives attached to a thing in her hands.

⚠️

Safety: Melt water spreads further than you expect and a hard floor gets dangerous fast, so keep the old towels down and mop between runs while Kreston is walking. Ice straight out of the freezer sticks to skin, so let the block sit a minute before she handles it. Single toy cars are choke-sized for him, so the fleet goes back up on the table between runs. Buckeyes and acorns are the same size in his mouth, and a chewed buckeye poisons a child, so the hunt bag stays on your shoulder and Kreston carries leaves and nothing else. The scissors stay with you.

Taping the Track Down the Hall

You need: 1 roll masking tape · 4–5 cushions.

  1. Run two lines of masking tape down the hall, a stride apart. She walks between them to check the width.
  2. Cushions along the track at intervals, one per station. She puts them where she wants them.
  3. Ask what each station is called. Hold the names in your head, because she writes them at 9:15.

The Hallway Railway

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 roll masking tape, 1 laundry basket, 6 feet of rope or a bathrobe belt, 4–5 cushions, on the track, Paper and 1 marker for the station signs, Real cargo: the washing, a bag of cans, a stack of books, 1 wooden spoon and 1 saucepan for the whistle

  1. Tie the rope to the front of the basket and put the free end in her hand. She is the engine, the basket is the wagon.
  2. Mark each station with a cross of masking tape beside its cushion, so the stops stay put once the cushion gets kicked.
  3. One sign per station. She draws, you write the name she gave you underneath, and each sign leans on its cushion.
  4. Load the washing and haul it to the station nearest the machine. It comes out of the basket and waits by the door.
  5. Second run, the cans to the cupboard. Third run, the books to the shelf. Every trip carries something that had to move anyway.
  6. Bang the wooden spoon on the saucepan at each station. She will want that job, so hand it over on run two.

💡Real cargo is the whole difference. A basket of nothing gets abandoned at station two. A basket with the cans in gets dragged the length of the house four times.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Barrow Full of Leaves

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Rake the leaves off the path into one heap, load them into a wheelbarrow, a laundry basket or two grocery bags, and let her wheel the lot to wherever they go. She will tip half of it out on the way and want to jump in the rest, both of which are fine. Load it twice.

🎨 MAKE
Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Two Ways to Shift the Same Load

Six cans weigh the same whatever they travel on. Her arms are about to tell her something else, and finding that out is worth the afternoon.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 old towel or blanket, The laundry basket, The rope, 6 heavy things: cans, books, a bag of potatoes, 1 roll masking tape for the finish line, A stretch of carpet and a stretch of bare boards or vinyl, whichever the house has, A stopwatch, or the timer on your phone

  1. Tape a finish line across the far end of the hall, and a second one the same distance down the carpeted room. Each course starts at a door.
  2. Pile the six heavy things onto the blanket. Cans, books, potatoes, all of it.
  3. She takes a corner and drags it the length of the carpet. Start the timer and say the number out loud when she crosses the tape.
  4. Same blanket, same load, down the hall boards this time. Time it again. The floor changed and nothing else did.
  5. Move the same load into the basket, tie the rope back on, and send her down the hall again. Time that too.
  6. Ask her which was hardest, take her answer as it comes, then ask what the basket does for her that the blanket does not.
  7. Let her load it herself and run it as often as she likes. Stop timing once she stops asking, and on the last run she sits in the basket and you pull. She has earned that.

💡Load it heavy enough that the blanket run is hard work. A light load slides fine on anything and teaches her nothing.

The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 41Day 284 · afternoon →
Finished result d284-result.png
✨ Afternoon alternatives
  • One journey, one basket, one heavy thing.
  • Drag the blanket with a doll on it and nothing else.
  • Move every book in the house to a new shelf.
  • Pull each other up and down the hall and stop there.
🌳 Out again · pick one
  • The riverside path, and today is Indigenous Peoples' Day, so tell her in one sentence who lived along this water first
  • The neighborhood park, kicking through whatever the wind brought down
  • The woods loop, hunting for the first bare tree
  • A walk to the recycling bins with everything the railway carried
Day 284 · For the grown-up Moving Day · Monday, October 11
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, which is the whole job description this morning. Give him a small bag and let him carry leaves from the heap to the barrow, one fistful per trip. He will do it for longer than you expect, and the walking-while-carrying is the part he is working on.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He has ten words at 16 months and more is often one of them, so give it something to attach to: put one can in the basket, pull him two steps, stop. He asks. You go again. That exchange is worth more to him this afternoon than the ride is.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Heavy pulling settles her faster than any conversation about the noise does.

A child kept indoors on a wet October Monday gets loud, clumsy and quick to cry. She needs pushing, pulling and carrying to feel where her limbs are, and a warm carpet gives her nothing to push against. Hauling a basket of cans the length of the hall delivers that load through her shoulders, hips and hands, which is why she comes back down after it and why an hour of screen time leaves her worse. Talking to her about the volume asks the part of her that is already flooded to do more work. Give her something heavy to move first, then say the thing you were going to say.

⚠️

Safety: The rope stays in a hand, hers or yours, and goes back in the drawer the moment you stop, never left slack or in a loop on the floor. A loaded basket dragged down a hallway does not stop for a 16-month-old, so Kreston rides in the basket or waits behind a door, never underfoot. Socks on taped floorboards slide, so put her in bare feet.

Prep for Day 285

Leave the dirty washing in the basket instead of the machine, and stand the basket, the rope and a roll of masking tape by the hall door.

The Headlight Test

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 flashlight, plus your phone flashlight as backup, The four foil signs from this morning, Kitchen foil, 2 spare pieces of cereal-box card, 1 roll masking tape, 1 permanent marker, 1 blanket or towel for the window, The fleet and the box car

  1. Clear the floor of everything that is not a car, then tape the blanket over the window and shut the door.
  2. Hand her the flashlight. The fleet is at the far end of the room and she finds it with the beam.
  3. Hold the flashlight low, at the height of a car's own headlights, and drive one car up the room. Then hold it high and look at what changed.
  4. Point the beam at the foil signs from across the room. The foil throws it straight back, and she will say so before you do.
  5. Make two more on the spot: spare card, a patch of foil taped on, a shape in marker. She stands them where she wants and tests them from the door.
  6. Put her in the box car with the flashlight and let her drive the dark room. Your phone flashlight is the streetlight, on the floor, pointing up.

💡Give her the flashlight and keep your hands off it. Half of what she is learning is that the beam goes where she points.

The Reflector Hunt on the Curb

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

The clocks go back at the start of November and the light is going by half past six, so spend this one counting what is built to be seen in the dark. Bike pedals, the reflectors on a trash can left out for pickup, the strip on a mail carrier's coat, the red plastic on the back of every parked car. She finds five before you turn for home.

The Tunnel Under the Table

The dark space under the dining table has been catching her eye all week. Two blankets over the top turn it into somewhere she drives through and then stays.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: The dining table, 2 dark blankets or a duvet cover, 4 clothespins or bulldog clips, 3–4 cushions, The flashlight, The fleet, 4 books, A snack and a drink in a lidded cup

  1. Drape both blankets over the table with two opposite ends left open. That is the tunnel.
  2. Clip the blankets to the table legs with the clothespins so it survives being crawled through.
  3. Cushions down the middle as the floor, leaving a clear run for the cars.
  4. She drives the fleet in one end and out the other by flashlight, one car at a time.
  5. Send a car in and let her find it with the beam from outside. Then she hides one for you.
  6. Snack and the lidded cup go in. Eating under a table is most of the appeal.
  7. Four books in and the flashlight on. Read one lying down, then leave her in there.

💡Take the tunnel with you to the pool as a promise. She comes out of the water quicker when there is somewhere to go back to.

Day 285 · For the grown-up Headlights · Tuesday, October 12
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, and the light switch is the chore he wants most. Hold him up to it and let him work it: on, off, on. Say the words with the flick rather than after it, because he is matching sound to event all day.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 16 months he walks and stands on his own, which changes what the pool asks of him. Keep a hand on him on the tiles, hold him upright in chest-deep water and let him march on the bottom. Twenty minutes and out, wrapped up before he cools.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A darkened room helps more than a quiet one.

Azlyn gets wound up and nothing lands, so you take the noise down. Try the light instead. Vision takes the biggest share of what her brain is handling, and dropping the room to one flashlight beam cuts most of that input at a stroke, which is why a fort, a tunnel or a parking lot under a blanket settles her inside five minutes. The beam also gives her one thing to attend to and permission to ignore the rest. Anything that has to be talked through goes better under a table with a flashlight than at a bright kitchen table.

⚠️

Safety: Small flashlights and bike lights run on button batteries, and a swallowed one burns through a child's throat within hours. Check that every light you hand her has a battery cover screwed shut, and keep loose batteries off the floor. Clear the floor before you darken the room, and keep the box car on the level and nowhere near the stairs while it is dark, because it hides her feet. Keep the table blanket clipped where Kreston cannot pull it down onto himself. Reflectors live at the curb, so Kreston walks on your hand or rides with the stroller brake on, Azlyn stays on the house side of you, and you both stop at every driveway to look before you cross it. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

Every Part She Can Name

  2. She will run dry at about six. Turn the vehicle over and let her find three more underneath.

The Car She Draws Twice

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 3 sheets of paper, plus spares, Pencils and crayons, 1 toy vehicle, 1 magnifying glass, or a jam jar of water, Masking tape, to hold the paper down

  1. Tape a sheet of paper down in front of her and put the vehicle out of sight. She draws it from memory, and you say nothing at all while she works.
  2. Write MEMORY on the back in pencil and set it aside face down.
  3. Stand the vehicle on the table where she can see it, tape down a second sheet, and let her draw it again with the real thing in front of her.
  4. Hand her the magnifying glass, or stand the jam jar of water behind a wheel so it swells. Give her the tread, the axle, the seam down the middle of the roof.
  5. Third sheet, wheels only, as big as the paper goes. Nothing else on the page.
  6. Lay the first two side by side and let her tell you what is on one and missing from the other. Write her sentence under the second drawing word for word.

💡Resist naming the parts she has left out. She finds them through the glass, and a part she found stays hers.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Counting Wheels From a Bench

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the nearest bench to a road and sit on it for twenty minutes with nothing to do but count wheels. Cars have four, bikes have two, the stroller has four small ones, and the garbage truck has more than either of you can count from a bench. She will want to run after ten minutes, so walk a loop and come back to the same bench for a second sitting.

The Spotting Book

She has drawn the same vehicle three times today. Now she makes a book with a different one on every page, small enough to go in a bag and out of the house.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half, 1 stapler (you hold it), or string and a pencil to punch the holes, Crayons, 1 marker, 1 pencil for the ticks, 1 small bag she carries it in

  1. Fold the three sheets together in half and let her run her thumb down the crease.
  2. Staple the fold three times while she holds the pages square, or punch two holes with the pencil point and tie the string through.
  3. One vehicle per page. She draws them all: car, bus, truck, bike, tractor, whatever she saw from the bench.
  4. Caption each page in her words with the marker, underneath the drawing. Her spelling and her grammar, not yours.
  5. Leave the last page blank for something she has not seen yet, and tell her that is what it is for.
  6. Book in the bag, pencil in the bag, and walk to the library. She ticks a page every time one goes past.
  7. At the library, find a book with the vehicle she could not draw in it, and borrow that one.

💡Keep the book in the bag by the door all week. It goes out with you tomorrow, and the ticks are what make it hers.

Day 286 · For the grown-up The Slow Look · Wednesday, October 13
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and points at what he wants named, so a bench by a road keeps him busy. Say the whole word back with one more attached (a bus, a red bus). At ten words and climbing, his half of the exchange is the point, so leave gaps he can fill.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He is 16 months and copies chores, so let him hand his own book over at the desk. Board books are for chewing at his age and the library knows it. Sit him in the picture-book corner and let Azlyn choose his for him, which she will take more care over than choosing her own.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Close looking is the one thing a tired child can still do.

Some days Azlyn has nothing in the tank for building, running or being reasonable, and a magnifying glass and one object will still hold her for twenty minutes. Looking hard asks almost nothing of her body and a good deal of her attention, which is the ratio a flat day needs. It also feeds the thing her drawing is short of: children draw what they know rather than what is in front of them, and the only route from one to the other runs through looking at the real thing for longer than feels necessary. Keep the glass in the kitchen drawer.

⚠️

Safety: The bench sits at a curb, so Kreston walks on your hand or rides with the stroller brake on, Azlyn sits on the house side of you, and neither of them steps off the sidewalk after a wheel. The walk to the library goes the same way. The stapler stays in your hand and goes back in the drawer the moment the book is bound, and any staple that misses gets picked off the floor before Kreston is down there. Single toy cars are choke-sized for him, so the model vehicle stays on the table and out of his reach. A jam jar of water is glass, so stand it well in from the table edge.

One Road Through the Whole House

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 roll masking tape, The week's builds: the parking garage, the foil signs, the station cushions, the box car, Flattened cardboard offcuts, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), 1 permanent marker, Paper for the signs

  1. Start at the parking garage. Tape two lines out of its bottom ramp, a car's width apart, running towards the first station cushion.
  2. Where the road meets a doorstep or a gap, cut a bridge from the cardboard offcuts and tape it flat at both ends.

The Shop at the End of the Road

A shoebox on its side at the far end of the hall gives the road somewhere to deliver to, and her a reason to drive it forty times.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 11 items

You need: 1 shoebox, Paper, 1 marker and 1 roll masking tape, 20 bottle caps or buttons as the coins, 1 jar with a lid, for the coins, 1 toy truck, or a small box on wheels, 6 cans and boxes from the cupboard, Your actual shopping list pad, Thick card, 1 sheet, October's handprint, Washable poster paint and 1 wide soft brush, 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl, 1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month

  1. Set the shoebox on its side at the far end of the road. She writes the shop's name on paper with the marker and tapes it up, then stocks it from the cupboard: six real cans and boxes, arranged how she wants them.
  2. Price each one in bottle caps. One cap, two caps, three. Her prices, and they make no sense.
  3. Load the truck at the parking garage end and drive the delivery the length of the road. Unload, restock, go again.
  4. Swap over. You shop, she serves, and she counts the coins into her hand out loud.
  5. Get the pad out. She dictates the shopping list for the 2:30 trip and you write every item she says, including the ones you will not be buying.
  6. Count the bottle caps back into the jar before you leave and put the lid on.
  7. The October handprint sheet comes out last. Kreston goes on it first while he is calm, the washcloth already in your other hand. Then Azlyn on the same sheet beside him. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write October, her 3 and his 16 months beside the pair. If you are marking the frame this month, this is the afternoon for it: both of them against the door frame, a pencil line each, with the name and the date beside it.

💡Buy one thing off her list at the store, whatever it is. She spends the trip watching to see whether her list counted.

Day 287 · For the grown-up Everything Joins Up · Thursday, October 14
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and carries things while he walks, which is most of what he is practicing. Give him one big leaf for the walk to the tree. He arrives with it, shows you, and drops it. Bring a spare. The buckeyes stay in the bag with you, because every one of them is a choking size at 16 months.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He copies chores at 16 months, so give him the lightest real job in the store: one packet to hold from the shelf to the cart. He will carry it the whole way round. At home he hands things up to Azlyn while she puts the shopping away.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Mid-autumn is a low-energy stretch, and lowering the bar is the right response.

The run from the end of the light to the clocks changing is the flattest of the year for small children, and Azlyn is in the back half of it. The light drops, the first colds arrive, and the novelty of the season has gone. A three-year-old in that stretch does less, asks to be carried more and comes apart over a sock. Halving the plan is the accurate response rather than the lazy one: she gets the same hours with you and fewer demands inside them. Today joins up things she already built and asks almost nothing new of her. Do that on purpose.

⚠️

Safety: Bottle caps and buttons are the exact size that blocks a 16-month-old's airway. The coins come out only while you are at the store counter with them, and they get counted back into the jar and onto a high shelf before Kreston is loose in the room. The scissors stay with you.
