Day 288
The Rocket in the Hallway
The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 41Day 287 · for the grown-up
October · Week 42

Space Explorers 🚀

October 15 – October 21, 2027 · Days 288–294

Azlyn builds a rocket she can sit inside on Friday, and it stands in the hallway until Thursday. Everything after that feeds it: a sealed letter taped above the control panel, a tray of craters she makes herself, ten coins spent on supplies, a mission control desk at the far end of the hall, a shoebox of things you cannot get in space. She is running one long game across seven days and the box in the hallway is what holds it together.

No holiday lands this week, but two threads outlast it. The bulbs she plants on Tuesday come up in March, so the pot by the back door becomes a five-month wait she checks on herself. Then on Thursday afternoon she picks three things out of the week's pile, walks them round to a neighbor and knocks on the door. Leave the rocket standing as long as she wants it, even when it is in the way of the stroller.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Changing one thing at a time. Drop height, balloon size, parachute width. She predicts the result, tests it, and puts the two outcomes side by side.
  • Counting out money that runs out. Ten coins, priced goods, a shelf longer than the purse, and the choice about what goes back.
  • Reading a sequence of pictures left to right. The recipe card tells her what to do next, and she ticks off where she has got to.
  • Depth, spacing and waiting. Bulbs set three deep and a fist apart, then five months of nothing happening above the soil.
  • Speaking to somebody who is not you. Dictating a letter, calling a checklist the length of the hall, saying her own line on a doorstep.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 16 months this week. He stacks four blocks, copies whatever chore is in front of him, and has ten words or so. He carries leaves to the pile, posts offcuts through the rocket window, and hands you every stone on the sidewalk.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 42 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 42 · read it on Day 288

The Pictures People See in the Sky 🌌

Seven bright stars sit above the house tonight, and the picture drawn round them depends on who is looking. British families call them the Plough, American ones the Big Dipper, and in France the same seven are a saucepan. Aboriginal astronomers in Australia look at a different part of the sky altogether, and they read the dark dust lanes of the Milky Way rather than the stars. The shape they find in the gaps is an emu.

✨
Try it

Spoon yogurt into a bowl and drop seven blueberries on top in the Big Dipper's shape, four for the bowl and three for the handle. She eats the handle first.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 42 · around the world →
Around the world w42-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • A letter teaches her that writing is aimed at someone
  • Borrowing and returning is her first experience of trusted ownership
  • Money is a story about exchange long before it's arithmetic
  • Your own day's work is more interesting to her than you think
  • Children learn to care about a place by improving it
  • Reading a recipe is her first experience of print that tells you what to do
  • Handing something over in person is a separate skill from making it
Did you know

The Emu in the Sky is made of the gaps, so you find it by looking at the dark.

The Cone on Top

You need: the big box · 1 sheet thick card · 1 roll masking tape · 1 roll kitchen foil · 1 permanent marker.

  1. Roll the card into a cone, wide end down. You hold the point, she tapes the seam and then the rest of it however she likes.
  2. Wrap the cone in foil and let her press it down onto the card. The creases stay in.
  3. Stand it on top of the box and step back with her. Ask what the box has to become for a nose cone to make sense, and write her answer on the side in marker.

The Rocket She Fits Inside

⏱️ 60 min🧰 9 items

You need: 1 large box, tall enough for her to sit up in, 1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only), 2 sheets thick card: this morning's cone, and one for the fins, 1 roll masking tape, 1 roll kitchen foil, 1 permanent marker, 4–6 bottle caps or buttons for the panel, 4–6 heavy books to weight the base, 1 cushion for the floor of it

  1. Run your hand round the inside of the box for staples. Then let her sit in it and mark the door and the window from the inside, in marker.
  2. Cut the door on three sides so it swings, and the window where she marked. She stands back while you cut, and the knife goes back on the shelf between cuts.
  3. Lay the books flat in the bottom around the edges and the cushion on top of them. The base is heavy now and the box takes her weight.
  4. Tape the cone on. Cut two fins from the second sheet of card and tape them low on the outside, on the sides she picks.
  5. She draws the control panel inside the door. You tape the bottle caps on as switches, proud of the card so they move under her thumb.
  6. Get out and leave her in it. Wrap a band of foil round the outside if she wants one. The rocket stands in the hallway until Thursday.

💡Tape the tops on loose enough to rock. She presses them all week.

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Kick the fallen leaves into one heap in the yard or the park. Mid-October is when the big trees let go, so the pile builds fast. Count down from ten and she jumps in on zero. Build it back up and go again.

The Message She Sends to Space

Somebody finds the rocket one day and works out who lived here. Azlyn decides what they get told.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 4 sheets plain paper, 1 envelope, Crayons, 1 marker, Masking tape, The rocket from this morning, standing in the hallway, Your phone, to photograph every page before it is sealed

  1. Sit on the floor with the paper and ask what a stranger should know about this house. Write it word for word, wrong grammar and all.
  2. Read it back in her own words. She will correct you, and the correction goes in too.
  3. Second sheet: she draws everyone who lives here in crayon, and you write the names underneath as she tells you who is who.
  4. Third sheet is the house from outside. The fourth is hers, for whatever she wants on it.
  5. Photograph all four pages before anything gets folded.
  6. Fold them into the envelope and seal it. She writes on the front in marker, and that is the address.
  7. Tape the envelope inside the rocket, above the panel, where she can see it and not reach it.

💡Kreston will come out bigger than the house and you will have no arms. Leave both.

Day 288 · For the grown-up The Rocket in the Hallway · Friday, October 15
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores. Hand him one fistful of leaves at a time to carry to the pile. By the third go he says the last word of the countdown with you. Keep him to the side of the heap she jumps into.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Give him the offcuts from the door and the window. At 16 months he posts things through gaps. Hold a scrap to the window hole, let him push it through to Azlyn inside, and she hands it back.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A letter teaches her that writing is aimed at someone.

Azlyn has watched you write for two years without seeing where any of it goes. An envelope closes that loop. She dictates, watches her own words turn into marks on a page, and the marks then travel to a person who is not in the room. Children dictating to an adult produce longer and better organized sentences than they can write for years afterwards, because someone else carries the mechanics. Naming the reader before she starts changes what she chooses to say, and sealing the envelope in front of her fixes the idea that writing is a thing you send.

⚠️

Safety: The craft knife and heavy scissors are adult-only and go back on the shelf between cuts, not the arm of the sofa. Check inside the box for staples before either child touches it. A tall box tips, and Kreston walks now and will pull on it, so keep the books in the base and keep him out of the rocket while she is climbing in and out. Bottle caps and buttons are the size Kreston chokes on at 16 months, so they stay in your pocket until each one is taped down, and you run a thumb along the row every morning the rocket stands in the hall and press any loose one back down.

Sifting the Moon Dust

You need: 1 old sheet or towel · 1 deep roasting pan · 8 cups all-purpose flour (1 kg) · 2 tbsp cocoa powder · 1 sieve.

  1. Spread the sheet on the kitchen floor and stand the pan in the middle. Everything happens on the sheet today.
  2. She sifts flour through the sieve into the pan until it lies two fingers deep, then smooths the top with the side of her hand.
  3. Sift the cocoa over the top so the whole tray goes gray. Leave it untouched until 9:15 and tell her nothing about what comes next.

The Craters She Makes Herself

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: The sifted tray of moon dust, on its sheet, 5–6 stones and marbles in different sizes, a golf ball if you have one, 1 sieve, 1 small pitcher of spare flour and 1 tbsp spare cocoa for the rebuild, 1 spoon and 1 empty cup for fishing the stones back out

  1. Kneel her at the edge of the sheet. Drop one marble from a hand's height and look at what it leaves: a hole, a rim, pale flour thrown across the dark cocoa.
  2. Same marble, dropped from as high as she can reach. Put the two holes side by side and ask which one came from higher up. The tray answers for her.
  3. Now change the other thing. Biggest stone and smallest stone, both from the same height she used last time. She will tell you which one mattered more.
  4. Fish every stone and marble out with the spoon, counting them into the cup.
  5. Rebuild: sieve spare flour over the tray, smooth it, dust the cocoa back on. A minute's work and she has a clean moon.
  6. Then let her drop everything she is allowed to drop, in any order, until the tray is holes on holes.

💡Say nothing between drops. The tray keeps every crater, so all four are still in front of her when you get to the rebuild.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Moon Rock Hunt

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a bag out and collect stones, one rule only: bigger than her fist. Weigh them two at a time in her hands and keep both, saying which is heavier each time. Come home with five and line them up on the step, lightest to heaviest. October drizzle helps: a wet stone shows its color.

The Flashlight She Has to Give Back

The good flashlight comes off the shelf on terms: it is yours, she can use it, it goes back at the end.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: 1 good flashlight with fresh batteries, 1 orange, or a ball about that size, 1 white plate, 1 chair, A dark hallway, or a room with the curtains shut

  1. Hand it over on those terms and let her carry it to the room herself.
  2. Shut the curtains and give her two minutes to sweep the beam round the walls. The novelty burns off fast and then she can hear you.
  3. Stand the chair in the middle, the white plate on it, the orange on the plate so it cannot roll. The plate throws light back up under it.
  4. She holds the flashlight to one side and lights half the orange. Put your finger on the line where the bright side meets the dark.
  5. Keep her flashlight hand still and walk a circle round the chair, saying what you see from each side: all of it lit, half, a sliver, none.
  6. Swap. She walks the circle while you hold the beam steady and calls out how much of the orange is bright from where she stands.
  7. Curtains open, flashlight off, and she puts it back on the shelf herself.

💡She will point it at your face. Turn your head, carry on talking, and it runs out inside a minute.

Day 289 · For the grown-up Moon Dust and Craters · Saturday, October 16
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and hands things over now. He picks up everything on the sidewalk, so take each one as it comes. Give him one stone too big for his mouth to carry to the bag.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At the lakeshore he heads for the water, so he stays inside your arm's reach the whole time you are near the edge. He is 16 months and stacks four blocks: pick him five flat stones wider than his own fist, well back from the edge, and let him build. He knocks it down himself and starts again.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Borrowing and returning is her first experience of trusted ownership.

Handing Azlyn the real flashlight, on terms, gives her something a flashlight of her own cannot. She holds a thing that stays yours, uses it under conditions she agreed to, and gives it back working. Three-year-olds sort ownership in stages: mine first, then yours, and last the awkward middle category of borrowed, which carries an obligation stretched across an hour. Saying the whole contract out loud in one sentence lets her hold all three parts of it at once. She puts it back on the shelf and finds out that being trusted with something is a thing she can do.

⚠️

Safety: Marbles and small stones are the right size to choke a 16-month-old, and they roll out of the tray. Count them in and out, work on the sheet, and sweep the floor before Kreston goes down anywhere near it. The only stones that go to him are the ones you hand him, every one of them wider than his fist. Loose flour travels, so keep it off the floor he crawls and walks on.

The Purse and the Price Labels

You need: 10–12 real things from the cupboards · sticky labels, or paper and tape · 1 marker · 1 tray.

  1. Walk the kitchen with her and let her pick what an astronaut needs. Take her choices at face value, including the can of corn.
  2. Write a price on a label for each, nothing above three, and she sticks them on. Say the number out loud as you write it.
  3. Line the shop up on the tray with the prices facing out. Tell her it opens at 9:15 and she gets ten coins.

Ten Coins for the Whole Mission

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 10 card coins, cut last night from 1 sheet of thick card, 1 paper bag or envelope as the purse, The 10–12 labeled supplies from this morning (rice, a washcloth, a can, a blanket, bandages), Spare sticky labels and 1 marker, for re-pricing, 1 tray or box as the shop counter, The rocket in the hallway, from Friday

  1. Set the tray on the table with you behind it. Count the ten coins into the paper bag out loud and hand it to her.
  2. Open the shop. Everything costs what its label says. She counts coins out of the bag into your hand, and you pass the goods across.
  3. She runs out. Hold the silence here and let her work at it, however long that takes.
  4. Then offer the rule that fixes it: anything she brings back, she gets the coins for. She chooses what she can do without.
  5. Second run, and the market changes. Re-label the blanket at five and the bandages at one, then let her look at the shelf again.
  6. Load what she bought into the rocket and count what is left in the bag with her.

💡Do not rescue her at the moment the coins run out.

The Planet Walk Down the Street

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Put a buckeye down at the front gate for the sun. Walk out counting paces and lay something at each planet: a stone for Mercury three paces on, a leaf for Earth at ten, an acorn for Jupiter fifty paces further than she expects. She gives up around Saturn. Pick it all back up on the way home.

The Balloon That Flies Down the String

A balloon lets its air out of the back and shoves itself forward. On a string, it goes where the string goes.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 6–8 balloons, 2–3 drinking straws, or a cardboard tube cut into short rings, 1 ball of string, 13 feet, Masking tape, 2 dining chairs, or a door handle and a chair, 1 clothespin or small toy as cargo

  1. Thread the string through a straw, tie it between the two chair backs and pull it tight, one end higher than the other.
  2. Blow a balloon up and pinch the neck shut. Do not tie it.
  3. Tape the balloon under the straw, neck pointing back at the high end. Two strips, one each side.
  4. She counts down from five and lets go. Every launch is hers to release.
  5. Change one thing at a time and run it again: fuller balloon, slacker string, both ends level. She calls it before each go.
  6. Tape the clothespin on as cargo and see whether it still makes the far end.
  7. Take the string down the second you finish, count the balloons back and pocket the lot.

💡She cannot blow these up and she will be furious about it. Give her the neck to pinch while you tape.

Day 290 · For the grown-up The Supply Shop · Sunday, October 17
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and walks the whole street now. Let him out of the stroller for the middle stretch and give him the leaf to carry, because the stones and the acorns stay in your hand. He passes it to Azlyn to put down.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Keep him out of the room while the balloons are up. Afterwards, give him the empty paper purse and a handful of jar lids too wide for his mouth. At 16 months he posts them in and tips them out again for five or ten minutes, then comes back to it twice more before dinner.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Money is a story about exchange long before it's arithmetic.

Azlyn cannot do the sum yet, but she can do the trade. She holds the whole idea that the coins go one way, the can comes the other way, and the coins are then gone. That last part is what shop play teaches and a piggy bank does not. Counting three coins into your hand also does more for her number sense than counting three of anything on a page, because each coin buys something and the total decides what she gets. Give her a fixed ten and let the shelf outlast them, and she meets scarcity in a form small enough to survive.

⚠️

Safety: A burst balloon is the worst choking hazard in the house for a child Kreston's age. Count the balloons, pick up every scrap the second one goes, and keep the pieces in your pocket rather than a trash can he can reach. Take the string down and put it away the moment you finish, because a line at toddler height is a strangulation risk. The card coins are mouth-size discs, so they stay up on the table with Azlyn and Kreston posts the jar lids, which are too wide for his mouth. Count all ten coins back into the bag at the end. Keep Kreston on your hand for every stretch of the planet walk he is out of the stroller, walk Azlyn on the house side, and stop at every driveway to look.

Two Cups and a Headband

The Desk with a Hundred Buttons

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 large box lid, or the flattened front of a box, 10–15 bottle caps or buttons, 2 wide jar lids and 1 spare strip of card, for Kreston's end, 1 roll masking tape, 2 markers, one of them red, The two headsets from this morning, 1 sheet of paper for the checklist, 1 flashlight as the warning light

  1. Lay the lid flat in front of her and leave it blank. She draws the dials, the screens, the numbers and one big red button in the red marker. You draw nothing on it.
  2. Tape the bottle caps on around her drawings, all ten or fifteen, so the desk has switches that move.
  3. Write the checklist on the paper with a small picture beside each line: door, cone, fuel, belt, go. The pictures are what she reads.
  4. Stand the desk at the far end of the hall from the rocket. Headsets on, one of you at each end, and you have to shout the whole length of the hall to be heard.
  5. Read the checklist one line at a time. She presses a switch for each and says done. The flashlight is the warning light: switch it on and she has to find the switch that puts it out.
  6. Swap ends and run it again, so she gets the desk and the seat.

💡Give her the last line of the countdown. A three-year-old who says go stays in a game twice as long.

The People Already at Work

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Monday morning, and half the street is at work before you leave the house. Count the jobs going on: the garbage truck and the arm that lifts, a van double-parked with the back open, somebody up a ladder, the store pulling its shutters up. Ask what each job is for. Mid-October gives you everybody's breath in the air.

Clocking On and Clocking Off

Azlyn works a real shift this afternoon: a start, a job list, a break, an end, and a look at where Joseph is while she does it.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 clipboard, or a piece of card and a bulldog clip, 4–5 sheets of paper, 1 marker, 1 kitchen timer, or the clock on the stove, The mission control desk from this morning, at the far end of the hall, A photo of Joseph's workplace on your phone

  1. Clip a sheet on the board. Write START at the top and the time next to it, and she says when the shift begins.
  2. Draw five jobs down the page as small pictures: check the door, check the cone, count the supplies, fill in the log, press the red button. She ticks each one with the marker as she finishes it.
  3. Set the timer for twenty minutes and leave her at the desk to work.
  4. When it goes, that is her break. Sit down with a drink and show her the photo of where Joseph is standing right now, and what he is doing at this hour.
  5. Second shift, and she picks two new jobs for the list herself, in her own marks, which you leave alone.
  6. Clocking off: she writes the end mark, unclips the sheet and hands it to you.
  7. She takes the log to the front door and props it where Joseph will see it the second he comes in.

💡Do not skip the break. Sitting down because a timer said so is the part of a working day she has never seen.

Day 291 · For the grown-up Mission Control · Monday, October 18
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so a garbage truck is a whole movie to him. Stop the stroller and let him watch the arm go up and come down twice. He waves at the crew and they wave back.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Tape the two jar lids onto the spare strip of card and give him that at his own end of the room, well away from the desk. At 16 months he copies what he sees, so he presses whichever switch she pressed last. Give him one end of the log to carry to the door with her.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Your own day's work is more interesting to her than you think.

Joseph leaves and comes back and the middle is a blank to Azlyn. She fills it with whatever she has: a room, a chair, a vague sense of far away. Showing her one photo and naming what he is doing at that hour turns the blank into something she can picture and ask about, and children who can picture the work ask better questions about it for months. The shift structure does the rest. Starting, ticking things off, stopping for a break and finishing on purpose gives her the shape of a working day in ninety minutes, from the inside.

⚠️

Safety: Buttons and bottle caps are a choking size for a 16-month-old, so the desk itself stays at Azlyn's end and the only switches Kreston gets are the two jar lids, which are too wide for his mouth. Count the caps out at 9:15 and back onto a high shelf at the end, and run a hand over the floor he walks on. The markers go back on the shelf between shifts, out of his reach.

Counting Out the Bulbs

You need: 20–30 spring bulbs · 1 tray · 2 craft sticks · 1 marker.

  1. Tip the bulbs onto the tray and let her turn them over. Show her the pointed end and the hairy flat end, and which way up they go in.
  2. Count them into piles of five, out loud, and let her lose count and start again.
  3. She draws a flower on each craft stick and you write the date beside it. Then both of you wash your hands.

The Bulbs That Wait Under the Ground

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: 20–30 spring bulbs from the supermarket. No bulbs: split a garlic bulb into cloves and plant them the same way, which is no less real, 1 trowel, or a big metal spoon, 2 large pots, or a cleared patch of ground, 1 bag of potting soil, or the soil that is already there, 1 watering can or pitcher, The 2 labeled craft sticks from this morning

  1. She fills each pot two thirds full with the trowel while you hold it steady. By the second pot she gets more in than out.
  2. Show her the depth: a hole three bulbs deep. Stack three in your hand so she sees the measurement rather than hears a number.
  3. She digs, sets each bulb pointed end up and covers it. A fist apart, measured with her own fist put down between them.
  4. Press the top flat with both palms. Water until it runs out the bottom.
  5. Push the labels in at the front and tell her the month they come up: five months of nothing happening.
  6. Stand the pots where she walks past them every day, and walk her past again this evening.

💡She will want to dig one up next week to check. One pot is hers to dig, the other stays shut, and you hold that line all the way to March.

The Leaves Off Next Door's Path

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a stiff brush and do next door's front path as well as your own, having asked first. Sweep the leaves off the step into a heap at the top of the driveway, well back from the road, and let her do the last stretch on her own. Come past it after swimming and look at what the two of you changed.

The Box of Things You Can't Get in Space

A shoebox holds everything Azlyn would miss if she left. She fills it and you write her reason on each thing.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: 1 shoebox with a lid, 1 small jar with a screw lid, Paper and 1 marker for the labels, Masking tape, Whatever she picks up outside, Your phone, for the photo of the finished box

  1. Ask what she would miss most and write the list as she says it, in her order, with no steering.
  2. Five minutes out at the door with the box: a leaf, a stone, a handful of grass with soil on it.
  3. Fill the jar from the tap, screw the lid tight, tape round it. Water out of a wall is the strangest thing in there and she has never once thought about it.
  4. One thing from her own room goes in, her choice, and it stays in until Sunday.
  5. Label each thing with what she said about it. Read them back and let her change any.
  6. Lid on, tape round the outside, and she says what goes on the top.
  7. Photograph the box open with everything laid out, because the grass has about a week in it.

💡Ask what she would take for Kreston. She picks something for him without being asked twice.

Day 292 · For the grown-up Bulbs and the Blue Planet · Tuesday, October 19
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so he wants the brush more than anything else outdoors. Give him a hand brush of his own and let him push leaves wherever he likes. He follows Azlyn down the path doing his version of her job.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He comes to swimming and stays within arm's reach in the water, every second. At 16 months he walks the poolside and heads for the edge given a moment. In the water he copies, so blow bubbles where he can see your face and wait for his version.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Children learn to care about a place by improving it.

Azlyn sweeping a neighbor's path leaves her with something no conversation about kindness reaches. She looked at one specific step, changed it, and can see the change on the way past this evening. Three-year-olds attach to places through their own hands, which is why the pot she planted counts for more than the bed you planted, and why she will keep checking her bulbs for five months. Effort is what makes a place hers, and it works on somebody else's doorstep as well as her own. Do the work beside her and stay off the moral. The swept path and the buried bulbs carry it.

⚠️

Safety: Daffodil and tulip bulbs are poisonous if eaten and they look like small onions. Count them out, count them in, and keep the bag off the floor while Kreston is loose, because at 16 months everything still goes in his mouth. Both children get their hands washed after soil, before food. Sweeping a front path ends at a road, so the heap stops at the top of the driveway, Kreston brushes on the house side of you, and neither child steps off the curb. At the pool both children stay inside your arm's reach in the water the whole time, and armbands, rings and floats are toys, never safety equipment.

One Bowl for Every Picture

You need: the picture recipe card · 4 small bowls · 2 cups rolled oats (200 g) · 2 tbsp cocoa · 3 tbsp honey or corn syrup · 2 tbsp shredded coconut.

  1. Sit her in front of the card and go along the pictures with your finger, left to right. Read the pictures, leave the words.
  2. One bowl under each picture. She tips the oats in and levels the cocoa, you do the syrup, and the coconut goes in last.
  3. Line the four bowls up in the order the pictures give. Ask which comes first and let her move them if she disagrees.

Moon Rocks You Can Eat

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: The four measured bowls: 2 cups rolled oats (200 g), 2 tbsp cocoa powder, 3 tbsp honey or corn syrup, 2 tbsp shredded coconut, 5 tbsp butter (75 g), 1 large bowl, 1 small saucepan, 1 wooden spoon, 1 baking tray and baking paper, The picture recipe card and 1 marker for ticking off

  1. Butter and honey into the pan on the back burner, low heat, you at the stovetop and her the far side of the table. Off the heat the moment the butter has gone.
  2. Oats and cocoa into the large bowl. She stirs them together, then ticks that picture on the card.
  3. Pour the hot mix in yourself and stir it through. Hand her the spoon once the bowl is cool enough to hold with both hands.
  4. Line the tray. Wet hands, and she rolls lumpy rocks. Lumpy is the target, so leave the ugly ones as they come.
  5. Roll a few through the coconut for moon dust, and she ticks the last picture.
  6. Into the fridge for an hour. They belong to the afternoon, so say that now.

💡Let the first three fall apart. She finds the right squeeze by feel.

The Buckeye and the Leaf

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Find a low wall, one buckeye and one wide leaf. She holds one in each hand, arms out level, and drops both at once. The buckeye wins every time. Air slows the leaf. There is no air on the moon, so an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather there and they landed together. Collect a bagful of buckeyes on the way home.

Eating With Nothing on the Table

Afternoon snack, the way it works with no gravity. Everything gets taped down.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 4–6 freezer bags, 2–3 straws, 1 squeezy sauce bottle, Masking tape, 1 tray, The moon rocks from this morning, Yogurt, apple pieces and a drink in a cup

  1. Clear the table down to bare wood. Nothing stays on it that is not stuck to it.
  2. Tape the tray to the table by all four corners and push it. It does not move, and that is the rule for the rest.
  3. Yogurt into the squeezy bottle, apple pieces into one bag, moon rocks into another. She loads them.
  4. Tape each bag to the tray by one corner, and the straw and the cup as well.
  5. She eats the apple out of the bag with no hands on the bag, and the yogurt straight out of the bottle. No plates, no bowls, no silverware.
  6. Halfway through, let go of everything at once and see what stays put. The tape is the reason any of it works.
  7. Untape, wipe down, and ask whether she would want dinner like that every night. She will say no.

💡Give her the squeezy bottle for the drink as well as the yogurt.

👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months. Buckeyes are a choking size, so they stay in the bag with you and he gets leaves. Give him one to drop off the wall and hold his other hand. He drops, watches and wants it back.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He gets the same snack, untaped and on a plate. At 16 months he copies everything Azlyn does at a table. Give him a small pot with a lid to pull off and press back on, which is the job he wants at a table anyway.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Reading a recipe is her first experience of print that tells you what to do.

Most print in Azlyn's life describes things: a story, a label, a sign. A recipe on the wall gives instructions, and the instructions have to be followed in order or the thing does not work. Following a picture sequence left to right builds the habit reading needs long before letters do, and she gets the payoff on a tray an hour later. Ticking each picture as she finishes it adds the other half, tracking where she is in a sequence she cannot hold in her head. Leave the card up on the fridge and she will run it again on her own.

⚠️

Safety: Melted butter and honey leave the stovetop at scalding heat, so the pan goes to the back burner and she stirs the bowl, never the pan. Keep Kreston out of the kitchen while it is hot. Whole lumps are a choking size for him, so his portion gets pressed flat and broken small. If you swap in nut butter, check it against every allergy in the house first. The freezer bags stay taped to the tray or in your pocket, because a bag over his face is a suffocation risk and it takes seconds.

The Slow Way Down

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

  1. Cut a square out of a grocery bag, about the size of a dish towel, and four short lines of string a hand's length each. You cut, she flattens the square on the floor. The scissors go back on the shelf. Tape one string to each corner.

Knocking on the Door Herself

Azlyn picks something out of the week's pile and walks it round to somebody herself.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 5 items

You need: Her moon rock, a drawing, and the spare parachute, 1 paper bag, Paper and 1 marker for the label, Masking tape, Shoes and a coat

  1. Lay the week's things on the table and let her choose three to give away. Take her choices as they come, including the one you wanted to keep.
  2. She draws a picture for whoever is getting them, and that goes in the bag on top.
  3. She says who the bag is for. Write the name big on the paper, she tapes the label to the front.
  4. Practice once on the kitchen door. Knock, wait, and say the line she picks. Once through and then stop, because a rehearsed child freezes harder.
  5. Coats and shoes, and she carries the bag the whole way, including the stretch where it drags on the sidewalk.
  6. She knocks. Stand one step back and let the pause happen, however long it runs.
  7. Walk home in the dusk and let her tell you what they said, which will not be what they said.

Day 294 · For the grown-up Coming Home · Thursday, October 21
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months. The peg astronauts are choke-sized and the plastic square is a suffocation risk, so both stay with you. Give him a clean empty yogurt pot of his own to carry in one fist while he toddles after Azlyn. Every bag and offcut stays in your pocket.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Bring him on the walk round and let him hold one handle of the paper bag while Azlyn holds the other. At 16 months he has ten words or so, and one of them will come out on the doorstep. Keep him off the road side of the sidewalk.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Handing something over in person is a separate skill from making it.

Azlyn spent twenty minutes on the parachute with no trouble at all. Standing on a step while somebody looks at her is a different task, and she may freeze on it. Handing an object to a near-stranger asks her to hold a plan in her head, read a face, and speak while being watched, all at once, and three-year-olds run out of room. Rehearsing the knock once at the kitchen door gives her a script to fall back on. Letting the silence sit, rather than saying her line for her, is what makes the second delivery easier than the first.

⚠️

Safety: A plastic grocery bag over a 16-month-old's face is a suffocation risk and it takes seconds, so every bag and offcut stays with you and goes away the moment you finish. Cut the string lines short. Clothespin astronauts are choking size at 16 months, so none of them go to him and they get counted back into your pocket at the end. She drops from the top step with a hand on the rail, and nothing goes over while Kreston is on the floor below. The scissors stay with you.

Day 295
The Bug Book
The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 42Day 294 · for the grown-up
October · Week 43

Insects & Minibeasts 🐛

October 22 – October 28, 2027 · Days 295–301

Every day this week she goes looking for something small and alive, and every day she has to slow down to find it. On Friday morning she staples a bug book together, and it stays in her hand until Thursday. She draws into it, tallies into it, carries it to the library and packs it in a rucksack. The animals are woodlice, snails, worms, ants and the last slow wasps of October. The skill underneath all of them is holding still long enough to count the legs.

The week works its way outward and then back in. Saturday gives her one doormat of ground with a string round it, Sunday she digs down through that ground in layers, and Monday she builds an ant colony out of cardboard tubes on the kitchen floor. Tuesday she moves like the animals herself, Wednesday she keeps ten finds and walks the rest back outside, and Thursday she packs her own bag and leads you out of the door. Each afternoon takes the morning somewhere else: the hunt becomes a sorting sheet, the dig becomes a paint strip up the wall, the colony becomes a tea party with four cards on the table.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Counting legs to tell one animal from another. Six for an insect, eight
  • Recording a find on the spot. One page of the bug book per creature,
  • Searching a set area. A string round a patch and a hole dug in layers
  • Direction words. Forwards, back, round and past, given as instructions
  • Choosing ten out of forty. Holding two things side by side, picking one,
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 16 months this week. He stacks four blocks, copies a chore before he understands it, and has ten words or more to use on you.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 43 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 43 · read it on Day 295

Eating Insects, Everywhere 🦗

About two billion people eat insects, and most of them would find our fuss odd. Market stalls in Oaxaca, Mexico sell chapulines, grasshoppers toasted with lime, garlic and chili. Bangkok street carts fry crickets by the bagful. In Uganda and Zambia, grasshopper season arrives with the rains and everyone eats well for a couple of weeks.

✨
Try it

Ants on a log for the afternoon snack. A stick of celery, a line of peanut butter or cream cheese down the groove, raisins pressed along it. She counts the ants before she eats them.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 43 · around the world →
Around the world w43-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • A field journal changes how she looks as well as what she records
  • A boundary makes a familiar place interesting again
  • Excavation teaches her that finding is a process, not a moment
  • Children need to see the adults in their life get celebrated too
  • Direction words are harder than position words and they arrive later
  • Deciding what's worth keeping is harder than collecting it
  • A trip she packed for herself gets remembered differently
Did you know

A cricket turns its feed into meat about twelve times as well as a cow does, which is why cricket farms keep opening.

Folding the Bug Book

You need: 6 sheets of paper · 1 stapler · 1 marker · crayons.

  1. Stack the six sheets, fold the whole lot in half together, and press the crease flat under her palm.
  2. Staple three times along the fold. She lines the stapler up, you lean on it.
  3. Write AZLYN'S BUG BOOK across the front and hand her the crayons for the cover. The first page gets filled outside at 9:15, so leave the book shut.

The First Five Finds

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: The bug book from this morning, 2 clear jars with punched lids, 1 soft paintbrush, 1 old white plate or pale tray, 1 metal spoon, Pencils and crayons, A magnifying glass, or a jar of water held over the tray

  1. Out the back door with the kit. Hunt where it is dark and damp: under stones and pots, in the leaves piled against the fence, under the trash can lid.
  2. Move each find onto the pale plate with the soft paintbrush, or scoop it up with the metal spoon. A brush shifts a woodlouse without hurting it.
  3. Hold the magnifying glass over the plate, or stand the jar of water above it and let her look through the curve of the glass.
  4. The two she likes best go in the jars with the punched lids, on the windowsill, for this morning only.
  5. One page of the bug book per find, drawn in pencil and crayon while the creature is in front of her. Count the legs out loud and write the number on it.
  6. Five finds and stop. Empty both jars where they came from before lunch.

💡A woodlouse she is watching gets seven legs a side and a ridged back. A woodlouse she is remembering gets a circle and a smile.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Web Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Late October mornings hang the webs with dew and they show for an hour or two before the sun burns them off. Walk the hedges, the fence tops and the gaps in the railings, counting how many she finds before the corner. Look for the fat orb web with its owner head-down in the middle, then get her to blow on a strand and watch it shiver.

The Leg Count

Six legs makes an insect, and two columns on one big sheet is how she meets that rule.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 large sheet of paper, or a flattened cereal box, 1 marker, Crayons, Glue stick or masking tape, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), Old magazines or a supermarket catalog, The bug book, 6–8 toys with legs to count

  1. Rule a line down the middle of the big sheet with the marker. Head one side SIX LEGS and the other NOT SIX LEGS, with a fat six and a crossed-out six above them so she can read the columns herself.
  2. Open the bug book at page one. She counts the legs on her own drawing, out loud, touching each one. Her count picks the column.
  3. Line the toys along the bottom of the sheet and count those too. A horse, a dog and a spider all land on the right, which is the point.
  4. Go through the magazines and the catalog for anything with legs. You cut, she chooses. The adult scissors do not leave your hand.
  5. She sticks each cutting into its column with the glue stick or a loop of tape. Crooked is fine.
  6. Crayons for the gaps: she adds any find she wants on the sheet twice.
  7. Count both columns and write the totals big at the top.

💡She will put the spider in the six column. Count its legs together with your finger on each one and let the answer land on her.

  • Draw one enormous beetle across a flattened box.
  • Sort the toys by how they move: crawl, fly, run.

  • Playgroup, and let her take the bug book to show
  • A friend's garden, which has different stones to lift
  • The garden center, warm and full of pots with things underneath
  • A short walk to see whether the morning webs survived the day
Day 295 · For the grown-up The Bug Book · Friday, October 22
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies whatever job he sees. Give him a pale saucer with a leaf on it and he will carry it round the garden the way she carries her plate. He has ten words or more now, so say bug each time she finds one and wait.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

At 16 months he stacks four blocks and he will want the toys off the bottom of her sheet. Give him his own four to build with beside her. He copies chores now, so hand him the glue stick to carry over and the lid to press back on.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A field journal changes how she looks as well as what she records.

Handing her a book to draw in slows the hunt down. A three-year-old without one finds a woodlouse, shouts, and moves on inside four seconds. With a page to fill she stays with the same animal for minutes, and to draw it she has to settle how many legs it has, which end the head is, whether the back is smooth or ridged. Researchers who study early science learning find that recording moves children from spotting into observing. She will also go back to the book on her own this evening, which is more than any answer you give her out loud gets. The drawings will be unrecognizable, and the looking is what you were after.

⚠️

Safety: Live minibeasts go into jars today, moved with the brush or the spoon and never with bare fingers. October wasps and bees still sting, and a drowsy one on the ground is the one that gets grabbed, so you look over the ground before she kneels on it. Hairy caterpillars irritate skin, so those stay on the plate. Every jar lid and specimen is mouth-sized for a 16-month-old, so Kreston stays your side of the tray. Wash hands before anything reaches a mouth. The scissors stay with you.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

The Line Round the Patch

You need: 6 feet of string · 4 stones · the bug book and a pencil.

  1. Walk her around the yard in her coat and let her pick the spot, even if it is the paving by the bin.
  2. Lay the string in a rectangle the size of a doormat, each corner pinned under a stone. Inside the line is hers all morning, outside it stays untouched.
  3. Ask how many creatures live in there. Write her number at the top of a clean bug book page and pocket it.

The Doormat Patch

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 6 feet of string and 4 stones marking the patch, 1 old white plate or pale tray, 1 soft paintbrush, 1 metal spoon, 2 clear jars with punched lids, 1 flashlight, 1 bucket, The bug book and a pencil

  1. Kneel at the edge of the string with the bucket beside you. Every stone, leaf and stick she lifts goes in it, so it can go back where it was.
  2. Shine the flashlight under the lip of each stone before she moves it. Woodlice bolt for the dark the second the light hits them.
  3. Anything she wants a proper look at goes on the pale plate, moved with the soft paintbrush or lifted on the metal spoon.
  4. Two jars for the two she cannot stop watching. Lids on, punched holes up, in the shade.
  5. Tally in the bug book, one mark per creature. Compare the total with her guess; the real number beats it.
  6. Tip the bucket back inside the string, stones dark side down, and empty both jars where they were found. Leave the line out for tomorrow.

💡She will ask to move on at twenty minutes. Hold her there. Everything interesting turns up after that.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Snail Wall

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Find a damp shaded wall, the back of the shed, or the stones under an ivy tangle. Late October pushes snails into the cracks to sit out the cold and they stack up in clumps. Count the shells without prying any off, then let her run a finger round one spiral from the middle out.

The Patch in a Shoebox

The same square of ground gets rebuilt on the kitchen table, warm and dry, with everything in it made of dough.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 10 items

You need: 1 shoebox, 1 tub of soil, leaves, twigs and small stones from the patch, Salt dough (2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, 1 cup water), or modeling clay, Food coloring, or a spoonful of cocoa for color, 1 craft stick, Masking tape, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), 1 flashlight, 2 scraps of card for labels, 1 marker

  1. Tip the tub into the shoebox and let her lay it out the way it was outside: soil down, stones where the stones went, leaves on top.
  2. Knead the cocoa or a few drops of food coloring through the salt dough until it goes soil brown. Her hands, your patience.
  3. She rolls worms. Long ones, short ones, a broken one. The craft stick scores rings along each body and legs into the woodlice.
  4. Put them where they belong: worms under the soil, woodlice under a stone, a snail up the side. She decides, and she remembers.
  5. Cut a flap in the shoebox lid with the adult scissors, hinge it with masking tape and put the lid on.
  6. Write her words for two of the creatures on the card labels with the marker and tape one beside each.
  7. Lights off. She lifts the flap and shines the flashlight in, which is how the real patch has it all day.

💡Salt dough dries hard on a windowsill in two or three days and cracks if she plays with it wet. The worms stay bendy until Monday.

  • Roll worms and stop there.

  • A bus ride to nowhere in particular, the front seats, hedge height
  • The park, with the jars left at home
  • A thrift store hunt for a book with beetles in it

Day 296 · For the grown-up One Patch of Ground · Saturday, October 23
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores before he understands them. Hand him leaves one at a time to drop in the bucket and he will keep at it long after you expect. Sit him outside the string so the patch stays hers.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Keep him well clear of the salt dough. Give him his own lump of modeling clay at the far end of the table, big enough that it cannot go in his mouth, and he will pinch and flatten it beside her. At 16 months he presses down with a whole flat palm, so a soft lump gives him more than a stiff one.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A boundary makes a familiar place interesting again.

Azlyn has walked over that patch of garden a hundred times without looking at it. Put a string round it and it turns into somewhere. A frame gives her a reason to search where there is no obvious prize, and searching without a prize is most of what science is. The limit also does the work of an instruction without sounding like one, because a doormat of ground gives her nowhere else to go. The hour is the time you set aside rather than the time she holds still. Teachers run the same trick with a hoop thrown on a field, and ecologists count everything inside a meter square of wire.

⚠️

Safety: Salt dough carries a dangerous amount of salt for a 16-month-old and it looks like food. Keep it your end of the table, count what goes into the box, and store the patch high once it is dry. Wash both children's hands after the soil. The scissors stay with you.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Two Buckets and a Rule

You need: 2 buckets · 1 trowel or a large metal serving spoon · 1 old towel or a trash bag.

  1. Pick the spot together, somewhere nothing is growing, and spread the towel.
  2. Two buckets, two jobs: soil in one, stones and roots in the other. Say the rule out loud: all of it goes back in the hole.
  3. Hand her the trowel for the first cut of turf and she keeps it. She digs, you keep one side of the hole cut straight.

Reading the Side of the Hole

⏱️ 60 min🧰 10 items

You need: 1 trowel, or a large metal serving spoon, 2 buckets, 1 stick marked with tape at every hand's width, 1 spray bottle of water, or a cup to trickle from, 4 small pots, one for each band, 1 old white plate or pale tray, 1 soft paintbrush, 2 clear jars with punched lids, An old towel or a trash bag to kneel on, 1 pitcher of water and a hand towel

  1. Kneel on the towel and dig a hole the width of the trowel, with one side of it cut straight down and flat, the way a slice comes out of a cake. The spoil goes in the buckets.
  2. Wet that flat side with the spray bottle. The bands come up as the water soaks in: dark and crumbly at the top, paler and stonier under it, roots running through the whole thing.
  3. Stand the marked stick against the flat face. She counts the hand's widths from the grass down and says where one band stops and the next starts. Take her line.
  4. One trowel of each band into a pot of its own, stood along the towel in the order they came out. Those four pots paint the wall at 1:00.
  5. Anything alive comes off the face onto the pale plate with the soft paintbrush. Count out loud and say which band it lived in: top band, four woodlice. Two jars for the two she wants to keep watching.
  6. Fill the hole back in from the buckets, deep soil first and turf last. Pitcher of water over four hands, then the hand towel.

💡Water is what makes the bands show. A dry face reads as one brown thing all the way down, and half a minute with the spray bottle turns it into a page.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Drumming Up the Worms

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the trowel to a patch of grass, push the handle a hand deep and drum on it, or rub a stick across it. The ground buzzes, worms read the buzz as rain or as a mole, and up they come. Give it five minutes. October grass after a wet week is the best ground for it.

The Soil Strip on the Wall

Everything she dug through goes up the wall in order, at her own height.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 strip of paper as tall as her, taped from kraft paper, wrapping paper or 4 sheets of letter-size paper, The 4 sample pots, one from each band, Brown, black and orange paint, or a mud and water wash, 1 wide brush, Crayons and paper for the drawings, Glue stick or masking tape, 1 marker, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only)

  1. Lay the strip on the floor and stand her beside it: it is her length. Rule it into bands with the marker, one per band from the hole.
  2. Stand the four sample pots beside their bands, in order, and open them.
  3. She paints each band with the wide brush in the color of the pot beside it. Dark at the top, drier and more orange going down.
  4. Crayons and paper while it dries: one creature per sheet, as big as she likes.
  5. Cut the drawings out with the adult scissors. She points at the band each one belongs in.
  6. She sticks them down with the glue stick and you write her words beside each in marker: worm, deep down. Woodlouse, top.
  7. Tape the strip to a wall with its bottom on the floor, so she has to crouch to see the deep end.

💡Let her paint past the lines and stop at four colors. Two browns and an orange say more than a neat gradient.

Day 297 · For the grown-up The Dig · Sunday, October 24
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and everything he finds goes to his mouth first. Give him the second bucket and a job on the grass well back from the hole: leaves in, leaves out, over and over. He brings you one every so often, which counts as sharing.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He gets his own strip of paper on the floor and one brush. At 16 months he paints in a fist grip and covers a hand's width before losing interest, so give him the mud wash and let him wear it. Tape it up beside hers at his height.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Excavation teaches her that finding is a process, not a moment.

Most of her hunting so far has been luck: turn a stone, there it is. Digging a hole in layers gives her something slower. She digs, wets the face, finds nothing, works again, and something turns up at the fourth go. That gap between effort and result is the part she has no practice at, and three is the age it starts being possible. Archaeologists and soil scientists both work this way, one measured layer at a time. Expect her to keep digging after you have had enough, which tells you the patience was there all along and needed something worth spending it on.

⚠️

Safety: Garden soil holds broken glass, cat mess and old slug pellets, so you turn the first trowel of every band over yourself before she puts a hand in. The trowel has a point and it stays pointing down. Hands get washed at the pitcher before anything reaches a mouth. Kreston eats what he digs, so he works his own patch of grass with an adult beside him. The scissors stay with you.

Opening activity · 8:00–9:00 AM

Four Rooms and a Tunnel

You need: 1 shoebox · 1 marker · 4 cardboard tubes.

  1. Stand the shoebox in front of her and ask what ants need where they live. Take her list as it comes.
  2. Draw four rooms in the floor of the box in marker: a nursery, a food store, a bedroom for the queen, a room for the trash.
  3. Lay the four tubes between the rooms as tunnels. Nothing gets taped yet. She can move them all morning.

The Nest Under the Lawn

⏱️ 60 min🧰 9 items

You need: 1 shoebox or shallow box, 6–8 cardboard tubes, Masking tape, Scissors or a craft knife (adult only), 1 marker, Cotton balls or torn tissue for the egg chamber, Torn paper scraps as the food store, Small toys, buttons or rolled paper balls as the ants, 1 sheet of brown paper or a flattened bag for the lawn

  1. Cut the tubes to the lengths she asks for and cut a doorway in one end of the box. You cut, she holds.
  2. Tape the tunnels down between her four rooms. Follow her plan, including the tunnel that goes nowhere.
  3. Cotton balls into the nursery, torn paper into the food store. Label every room with the marker in her words.
  4. The ants move in. Give each one a job out loud: this one carries, this one digs, this one feeds the babies.
  5. Lay the brown paper over the whole box as the lawn, taped along one edge so it lifts like a lid.
  6. Put it on the floor, lift the lawn, and let her run the colony without you.

💡Ants live underground because it is dark down there. Lift the lawn as little as she allows and the nest keeps its point.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Last Wasps on the Windfalls

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Go and find fallen apples, under a garden tree or on the grass at the park. Late October wasps are drunk on fermenting fruit and slow with the cold, and they cluster on the soft brown patches. Watch from a step back and count them. Turn one apple with a stick to see who else got there first.

The Workers' Tea

Ants have jobs and so does everyone here. Azlyn feeds the workers, and it lands on the table at half past three.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 9 items

You need: Bread, butter, and jam or cheese, 1 table knife, 4 plates and 4 cups, 1 pitcher of juice or water, Fruit she can cut with a table knife, Card cut into 4 cards, Crayons and a marker, A tablecloth or a clean dish towel, Something from the yard for the middle of the table

  1. Tablecloth or dish towel on, four plates and four cups round the table. She decides who sits where.
  2. Butter the bread with the table knife and let her spread the jam or lay the cheese. Uneven is correct.
  3. She cuts the soft fruit with the same knife, sitting down, both hands on the table.
  4. Four cards and the crayons. One per person in the house, drawn by her. You write the names in marker where she points.
  5. Something green from the yard down the middle of the table, laid out by her.
  6. She pours the juice into the four cups from the pitcher. Fill it a third full and it will survive.
  7. Half past three, everyone sits. She hands out the cards and says what each person carries all day.

💡Let her name the jobs herself. Her version of what you do all day is worth hearing, and worth writing down on the back of your card.

Day 298 · For the grown-up The Colony · Monday, October 25
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores before he understands them. Hand him tubes one at a time to carry to the box and he will keep the supply coming. He stacks four blocks now, so give him three spare tubes of his own while the box is still up on the table. The colony goes down on the floor at step six, and he goes in the high chair or out of the room from then on.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He gets a place at the workers' tea, a plate, a cup and a card of his own. At 16 months he has ten words or more, so name the food as it lands in front of him and wait for him to have a go. He will copy whatever Azlyn does with her cup, so watch which way round that goes.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Children need to see the adults in their life get celebrated too.

Most of the thanking in a house runs one way. Azlyn gets praised for putting her shoes on, and the person who found the shoes gets nothing. An afternoon where she butters bread for you, draws your card and says out loud what you carry teaches her something she cannot get from being thanked herself. She learns that the work around her is work, that the adults doing it are people, and that noticing is a thing you do on purpose. Gratitude at three grows out of practice rather than instruction, and an afternoon of laying places for other people is the practice. Keep the cards and date them.

⚠️

Safety: Drowsy wasps on fallen apples sting when they are trodden on or picked up, so the apples get turned with a stick and nobody goes barefoot on that grass. The table knife is blunt and still worth a rule: she cuts sitting down, at the table, with you beside her. Buttons are the size that blocks a 16-month-old's airway and the nest goes down on the floor at step six, so use the rolled paper balls or toys too big to swallow as the ants once it is down there. Kreston is in the high chair or out of the room the whole time the colony is on the floor, and any buttons get counted back into a tin and put up high. The scissors stay with you.

Worm, Snail, Beetle, Bee

You need: a clear stretch of floor · 1 sofa cushion · the bug book.

  1. Worm first. Flat on the carpet, no legs, stretch and pull the length of the room. Do it with her.
  2. Snail next, hands and knees, the cushion on her back as a shell, slower than she thinks she can go.
  3. Beetle high on hands and feet, then bee on tiptoes with her arms out. Open the bug book and let her pick two more. The route gets taped at 9:15.

The Arrow Course

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: 1 roll masking tape, 6 cards cut from a cereal box, 1 marker, 4–6 sofa cushions, 2 dining chairs, 1 box with both ends cut out, 1 broom, 1 scarf or a length of string

  1. Tape arrows along the floor to mark a route through the downstairs. She picks where it goes and you stick them down.
  2. Draw one creature on each of the six cards with the marker. Tape a card to the floor at each station along the route.
  3. Build the stations as you go: cushions to climb, the box to crawl through, the broom across the two chair seats to go under, the scarf stretched out as a line to walk.
  4. Run it once together. At every card she moves like that creature until she reaches the next one.
  5. Run it again while you count to twenty out loud. Slower is harder, so let the snail card cost her the count.
  6. Hand her the cards. She moves them, she picks the order, and you run the course while she watches.

💡The slow stations do the most for her. A three-year-old can sprint; holding a body still and moving it a hand's width at a time is the part she has to work at.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Wherever the Woodlouse Goes

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Lift stones until you find a woodlouse, set it down on flat ground and follow it. Walk where it walks, at its pace, and turn where it turns. She will last four minutes and cover a meter. Look at what it was heading for, which in late October is the nearest damp crack, and put it back there.

Telling the Beetle Where to Go

She has spent the morning being moved around by a taped arrow. Now she gives the directions and you do as you are told.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 1 large flattened cardboard box, 1 thick marker, 1 small toy beetle, or a pebble with legs drawn on, 8–10 bottle caps as obstacles, 1 leaf from the yard as the finish, Masking tape, Crayons

  1. Rule the flattened box into big squares with the thick marker, five or six across.
  2. Tape the leaf down in one corner as the finish and mark the beetle's starting square with a cross.
  3. Scatter the bottle caps over the board as stones the beetle has to get round. She places them.
  4. She sits on one side and tells you where to go: forwards, back, round it, past it, towards the leaf. You move the beetle as told, bottle caps and all.
  5. It will go wrong. Ask her what to say instead and wait, because she has the word somewhere.
  6. Color in every square the beetle crossed with the crayons, so the route she talked it through is there on the board.
  7. Swap. You give the directions and she moves the beetle, which is the harder half.

💡Take her words at face value even when you can see where she means. Following the instruction she gave is what shows her the instruction was short.

  • A café with a window and the bug book
Day 299 · For the grown-up Moving Like a Minibeast · Tuesday, October 26
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies whatever she does with his whole body. Let him have the box to crawl through once the course is clear, and hold the far end steady. He will go through it twenty times. Give him his own cushion on the floor to climb, well back from her run.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He has swimming too. At 16 months he walks the shallow steps holding your two fingers and would rather be upright than carried, so let him. Give him twenty minutes and get him out before he is cold. Never leave either child unattended near water, in the pool or in the changing room.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Direction words are harder than position words and they arrive later.

Azlyn has in, on and under down. She uses them without thinking, because they describe something that is sitting still. Forwards, back, round and past ask more: she has to hold a route in her head, imagine a thing moving along it, and pick the word that matches the movement. Left and right come later again, and often not until five or six. Her fumbling on the board is the work, and the fix is more chances to give instructions rather than a correction. Every direction you follow to the letter teaches her more than a right answer she copied.

⚠️

Safety: Chairs and cushion piles used as climbing stations tip over, so test each one with your own weight first and set the chairs on carpet rather than a wood floor. Kreston walks straight into a run like this at 16 months, so he runs it with you one station behind her, or goes in the high chair while she takes a turn on her own. Bottle caps are the size that blocks his airway and this board sits on the floor, so count them out and count them back into a tin, and he is in the high chair or out of the room the whole time the board is down. Take the scarf up the moment you finish. A length of string or fabric left on the floor is a strangulation risk for him. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

Emptying Her Pockets

You need: 1 tray · her coat and rain boots · the jars and pots from the week.

  1. Walk the house with the tray between you. Coat pockets, rain boot toes, the jars and pots on the windowsill, the shelf by the back door, under her bed.
  2. Tip the lot into one heap on the tray. Six days of shells, husks, feathers, legs and stones.

Ten Things and No More

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: The week's collection, 1 egg box, or a shoebox divided with strips of card, 1 tray, Card cut into 10 small labels, 1 marker, Cotton balls or torn tissue, Glue stick or masking tape

  1. Open the egg box next to the tray and count the holes with her. Ten holes, ten things, and the number does not move.
  2. She lines each hole with a pinch of cotton balls or torn tissue first, so the box is ready before the choosing starts.
  3. She picks. One thing per hole, her hands only. Keep your opinions off the gravel and the bit of chip bag.
  4. Ask what each one is and write her words on a label with the marker. Take them down as she says them, wrong names and all.
  5. Stick every label beside its hole with the glue stick or a loop of tape.
  6. Everything still on the tray goes back on the walk at half past ten. She carries the tray to the door herself.

💡Ten is the whole activity. Give her eleven and the box turns into storage, and the time she spends deciding is the part she will remember.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Returns Walk

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Everything that missed the box goes back where it came from, and she decides where that is. Late October will have swapped the ground since Friday, so the patch under the hedge is deeper in leaves and the stones are colder. Take the long way round and let her put things down one at a time. She will change her mind about two of them, so bring the tray.

The Three We Can't Name

Three things in that box have beaten everyone in this house. They get a real drawing this afternoon and a trip to the library for a name.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: 3 pieces of card cut postcard size, Pencils, an eraser and crayons, The 3 unnamed specimens, 1 jar of water, or a magnifying glass, 1 envelope or a paper bag, The library card, 1 marker

  1. Set the three specimens out with one card in front of each. One creature per card and no crowding.
  2. Hold the magnifying glass over the first, or stand the jar of water above it, and let her look before she picks up a pencil.
  3. She draws in pencil, with the eraser beside her. Count the legs, the wings and the body parts out loud while she works.
  4. Crayons last, for the colors. Ask what color it is rather than telling her.
  5. Number the cards 1, 2 and 3 with the marker and write her question on the back of each: how many legs? what is the shell for?
  6. Everything goes in the envelope with the library card, and she carries it.
  7. At the library she hands the envelope over and asks the question herself. Bring home whatever book has an answer in it.

💡Warn the librarian on the way in. Ten seconds of notice turns a puzzled adult into somebody who takes a three-year-old's questions at face value.

Day 300 · For the grown-up The Keeping Box · Wednesday, October 27
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and posting things into holes is close to his favorite job. Give him a spare shoebox and four blocks too wide for his mouth, well away from her tray, and he will fill it and tip it out for five or ten minutes, then come back to it twice before lunch. Nothing smaller than his fist goes near him.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Take him to the board-book corner and let him pull things off the low shelves. At 16 months he points at pictures and waits for you to name them, so sit with one book and name whatever his finger lands on. Let Azlyn choose his book and carry it to the desk.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Deciding what's worth keeping is harder than collecting it.

Gathering costs Azlyn nothing. She picks up everything, and by Wednesday there are stones in the washing machine. Ten holes and forty candidates asks her for something else: hold two things in mind, compare them against a reason, and let one go. Psychologists call this early executive function, and it is the same machinery behind waiting her turn and stopping a tantrum halfway through. She will not weigh them the way you would; the gravel wins because of where she found it. The reason matters less than the fact she had to have one, and a limit you hold to is what makes her produce it.

⚠️

Safety: One tray pools six days of gravel, husks, shells and legs, and every one of them is a choking size for a 16-month-old. The sorting happens at the table with Kreston in the high chair or out of the room, the tray and the egg box go up on a high shelf between rounds, and the floor gets swept before he is down on it. The jar of water is glass, so stand it well in from the table edge. The glue stick and the marker stay with you. Both children get their hands washed after the walk.

Only What Fits in the Rucksack

You need: 1 rucksack · the week's kit spread on the floor · 1 drink and 1 snack.

  1. Lay the whole week out on the floor: jars, brush, spoon, plate, bug book, pencil, magnifying glass, flashlight.
  2. She packs, and the drink and the snack go in last. Two rules only, that the bag shuts and that she carries it, so the tenth jar sorts itself out.

The Expedition She Leads

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: Her packed rucksack, 2 clear jars with punched lids, 1 soft paintbrush and 1 spoon, 1 old white plate or pale tray, The bug book and a pencil, 1 grocery bag to kneel on, Rain boots and a waterproof, A drink and a snack she chose herself

  1. Rain boots and the waterproof on. The bottom of an October hedge is wet all day and she will be down in it.
  2. She leads and she picks the turns. Walk behind her and let the route be hers, including the long way.
  3. At the wall or hedge she chose, spread the grocery bag and kneel on it. Rucksack off, kit out: plate, brush, spoon, jars with their punched lids loose.
  4. Shake one low branch over the pale plate and see what drops. Brush anything moving into a jar and lift the slow ones on the spoon.
  5. Bug book on her knee, pencil in her hand, drawn on the spot where she found it.
  6. Empty both jars back into the hedge bottom, then the drink and the snack sitting down before you head home.

💡Take a photo of her walking in front with the rucksack on. She looks at that one longer than any of the finds, and it goes in the bath-time slideshow tonight.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Long Way Home

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Come back a way she does not know, along the back of the houses or the far side of the green. Late October gives her the good ground for it: leaves to kick, puddles to check, bare brambles with the rose hips gone red on them. Let her decide at each junction and follow her even when it adds fifteen minutes.

The Plate of Things With Legs

Every minibeast of the week gets rebuilt out of food, counted for legs, and eaten.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: Bread, crackers or rice cakes, Cream cheese, hummus or peanut butter, Raisins and grapes, 1 cucumber and 1 apple, Breadsticks or pretzel sticks, Dry spaghetti for legs and feelers, 1 chopping board and 1 table knife, 2 large plates

  1. Board on the table, everything else in a row along the side so she can see the whole supply.
  2. Bodies first: bread, crackers or rice cakes spread with cream cheese, hummus or peanut butter using the table knife.
  3. Legs next. Snap the dry spaghetti and push it in, or lay breadsticks either side. Six for an insect, eight for a spider, and she counts them on.
  4. She cuts the cucumber and the apple on the board with the table knife for wings, shells and heads. Raisins press in as eyes.
  5. Halve the grapes and put them out as beetle backs. Quarter Kreston's the long way before any of them leave the board.
  6. Each finished creature goes onto a big plate, and it only gets there once she has counted its legs out loud.
  7. Both plates on the table. She names every one before anybody is allowed to eat it.

💡Let her eat as she builds. Half of them go before the plate is full, and a creature she made and ate is doing the same job as one she photographed.

Day 301 · For the grown-up The Expedition · Thursday, October 28
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and walks most of a short trip if you let him set the speed. Take the stroller and expect it to come home empty of him and full of kit. Give him his own small bag with one thing in it, because carrying something while walking is the skill he is working on.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

He rides the market facing out and points at the stalls. At 16 months he has ten words or more, so name what his finger lands on and give him a moment to have a go at it. Hand him one thing to hold all the way round, and make it something he cannot bite through.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

A trip she packed for herself gets remembered differently.

Azlyn chose the kit, the destination and the route today, and you carried nothing but the phone. Children hold on to episodes they had a hand in shaping, because the planning gives them a version of the day to compare against what happened. She will tell this one back to you for weeks, and the details she keeps will be the ones she decided: the jar she almost left, the turn she took by the mailbox. Nothing about the morning was more educational than yesterday's, and the difference is that she was the author of it. Ask her tonight where you went and see whose version comes back.

⚠️

Safety: Whole grapes and any round food block a 16-month-old's airway, so quarter Kreston's lengthways every time, no exceptions, and keep the whole ones off the board while he is at the table. Nuts and peanut butter need checking against what he has had before. The table knife stays on the table and she cuts sitting down, with you beside her.

Day 302
The Diwali Doorstep
The Big Book of Little Days · October · Week 43Day 301 · for the grown-up
October · Week 44

Dinosaur Discovery 🦕

October 29 – November 4, 2027 · Days 302–308

The theme is dinosaurs and the work underneath it is color and shape. She mixes colors she cannot unmix, traces the edge of a cardboard dinosaur as long as the hall, sorts ten greens from palest to darkest, and turns notched pieces until they fit. Nothing gets cleared away. On Thursday the whole week goes up on one wall and she hands out tickets and walks people along it.

Three holidays land in the first four days. Diwali on Friday brings colored salt poured on the doorstep and salt-dough lamps on the windowsill. Halloween on Sunday gets a hooded top with card spikes and a newspaper tail, and a flashlight-lit hour finding out what color does in the dark. Día de los Muertos on Monday sets a table for people who are not coming, with marigolds she dyes herself in a color she names. All three run on light and color, so the theme carries straight through them.

🧒 What Azlyn will learn
  • Mixing a new color and losing the old one. Red and blue make purple, and no amount of stirring gives her the red back.
  • Tracing a shape by its edge. One finger the whole way round the cut-out, nose to tail, which puts the shape through her hands.
  • Turning a piece until it fits. Notched cardboard joins one way only, so she rotates, tries, and rotates again.
  • Ranking greens from pale to dark. Sorting inside a single color word, much harder than telling green from blue.
  • Carrying one project across seven days. Friday's lamps end up on Thursday's wall, and she can point at how they got there.
👶 KRESTON THIS WEEK

Kreston is 16 months this week. He stacks four blocks, copies whatever your hands are doing at the worktop, and has ten or more words he uses on everything that looks close enough.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 44 · opener →
🌍 Around the world Week 44 · read it on Day 302

Dinosaurs Everywhere 🦕

Dinosaur bones have come out of the ground on all seven continents, Antarctica included. The largest so far came out of Patagonia in southern Argentina, where a farm worker found a thigh bone taller than a man. Mongolia's Gobi Desert gave up the first nest of eggs anybody had seen.

✨
Try it

Build a nest for dinner. Coil spaghetti into a ring on her plate and sit three boiled eggs in the middle for her to crack at the table.

The Big Book of Little Days · OctoberWeek 44 · around the world →
Around the world w44-world.png
👩 What you'll learn
  • Mixing colors is a lesson in irreversibility
  • Making the edges teaches shapes faster than naming them
  • Light changes what she thinks a color is
  • Naming a color she invented does more than learning the standard eleven
  • Fitting a shape into a hole is a test of mental rotation
  • Matching a shade is much harder than matching a color
  • Finishing something that took all week is its own lesson
Did you know

Birds are dinosaurs. The chicken in your fridge is a closer relative of T. rex than any crocodile is.
