The Colors That Won't Come Back

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: The 5 bowls of salt from this morning, Table salt, extra, in the box, Food coloring, red, blue and yellow, 5 lidded jars or zip-lock bags, 1 tablespoon and 1 teaspoon, 1 dark baking tray, or a sheet of black card, 1 dustpan and brush, 1 pitcher of warm water

  1. Tip three bowls into three jars. Three drops of red in the first, blue in the second, yellow in the third. Lids tight, and she shakes until the white is gone.
  2. The fourth bowl goes into the fourth jar. Two drops of red and two of blue on top of it, lid tight, and she shakes until it turns a color that is in none of the bottles.
  3. The fifth bowl into the fifth jar, red and yellow this time. She names both of the ones she made.
  4. Spoon a little of the purple onto the dark tray and ask her to get the red back out of it. She stirs with the teaspoon, and it stays purple.
  5. Out to the front door with the jars. Sweep the doorstep with the dustpan and brush, then trickle plain salt from the box into a circle with four petals.
  6. Hand her the jars one at a time to pour from. It stays all evening, then the pitcher of warm water washes it down.

💡Let her scrape at the purple for a full minute trying to get the red back, and hold off on the explanation.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Leaf Pattern by the Gate

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take a paper bag to the end of the street and fill it with fallen leaves, sorted into reds, yellows and browns as you go. At your own gate, clear a square of sidewalk and lay them in rings, darkest on the outside. Tell her the wind takes it tonight, before she starts.

Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

Pinching the Little Lamps

Salt dough wants two hours in a low oven. This goes in at half past one and paints at quarter past four.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 9 items

You need: All-purpose flour, 2 cups, Salt, 1 cup, Water, 1 cup, 1 mixing bowl, 1 baking tray and baking paper, Poster paint and 1 brush, 6 battery tealights (never real flames), 1 wet washcloth, 1 permanent marker

  1. Flour and salt into the bowl, water in last, and let her mix it with both hands until it stops sticking to them.
  2. Give her a lump the size of a plum. Thumb into the middle, then the walls pinched up and out into a small dish. Make one beside her to copy.
  3. Six on the papered tray, not touching. She presses a thumbprint into every rim so they are marked as hers.
  4. Oven at its lowest setting for two hours. Wipe her hands with the wet washcloth and shut the kitchen door behind you.
  5. Once they are out and cool, turn each one over and write the date on the base with the permanent marker.
  6. At 4:15 she paints them with the brush. Thick poster paint, straight on, no notes from you about which colors belong together.
  7. Drop a battery tealight into every lamp and stand them along the windowsill. Shut the curtains before dinner and turn the big light off.

💡Six is plenty. Walls thinner than her own finger crack in the oven, so say so once, then let two of them crack anyway.

  • Chalk the pattern on the path instead of pouring salt.

  • Meet a friend at the park, and take a jar of colored salt to give away
  • The park, before the light goes
  • The corner store, and let her choose something for tonight's table

Day 302 · For the grown-up The Diwali Doorstep · Friday, October 29
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so give him a paper bag and let him fill it with whatever he picks up. He tips it out on top of her rings, so build the pattern in two halves and let the outer one be his.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

The dough stays out of his hands today, so give him a job instead. At 16 months he copies chores, and a wet washcloth and a table to wipe hold him through the clearing up.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Mixing colors is a lesson in irreversibility.

Azlyn spends much of this year testing which actions run backwards. Water poured out of the pitcher goes back in it. A tower comes down and goes up again. Red and blue stirred together make purple, and no stirring gives her the red back, which is the first hard case she has met. Researchers working on this age find that undoing an action in your head arrives long after undoing one with your hands, so she needs the physical dead end before the idea holds. You gave her that dead end this morning and let her push at it. The colored salt out on the doorstep makes the same point, and none of it goes back to white.

⚠️

Safety: The oven is on low for two hours with Kreston copying everything that happens at a worktop, so keep him out of the kitchen while the tray moves. Salt dough and neat food coloring are both dangerous swallowed, so they stay at your end of the table and both children get their hands washed before they leave the room. Battery tealights only, because a house with a walker in it does not get an open flame at floor level.

Deciding Which Dinosaur

You need: a dinosaur picture book · 6 feet of string.

  1. Sit with the book and let her turn pages until she picks one. Her choice stands all day, so let it take as long as it takes.
  2. Stretch the string down the hall so she can see six feet. That is how long yours will be. Tell her the real one was five strings nose to tail and walk all five with her.
  3. Ask which wall he goes on, and hold your hand flat where his head will be.

Where the Dinosaur Stops

⏱️ 60 min🧰 7 items

You need: Flattened cardboard boxes, 4–6, 1 roll packing tape, 1 stick of chalk, light color, 1 permanent marker, 1 craft knife, or heavy scissors (adult only), The dinosaur picture from the book, 6 feet of string

  1. Tape the flattened boxes into one sheet on the floor, seams taped both sides. Lay the string on it to check he fits.
  2. Prop the book open beside her and let her chalk the outline, hands off however odd the legs come out.
  3. Go over her chalk line with the permanent marker so it survives the cutting.
  4. Cut along her line with the craft knife while she stands well back. The knife goes out of reach every time you stop.
  5. Now she runs one finger the whole way round the cut edge, nose to tail and back again. Every dip and spike, no shortcuts.

💡Your cutting takes four minutes and her edge takes twenty, and the twenty is the part she keeps.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Measuring the Dinosaur in Footsteps

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the string and the chalk to the widest stretch of sidewalk near you. Lay the string out, chalk a cross at each end, and let her walk heel to toe along it, counting out loud. Then walk it yourself and compare the two numbers, which will bother her. Late October takes the feeling out of small fingers in half an hour, so count first and argue on the way home.

Standing Him Up in the Hall

The cut-out gets a wall, a name and a neighbor her own height.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: The cut-out dinosaur, Packing tape and masking tape, 2 cardboard tubes, or 2 tightly rolled magazines, for splints, 1 permanent marker, 1 sheet of card for the name label, 1 pencil

  1. Hold him flat against the hall wall and let her walk his length, deciding which way he faces.
  2. Lay him face down and parcel-tape the two tubes along the back of his neck and tail as splints, flat to the card so nothing stands him off the wall.
  3. Masking-tape him to the wall at the head, the tail, both feet and twice along the spine. Flat against the bandage, never propped, and press every edge down hard so he holds until Thursday.
  4. She names him. Write it on the card in marker, in her own words, and tape it up at her eye height.
  5. Stand her beside his front leg and pencil a line at the top of her head, with her name and the date.
  6. Mark his height in the same pencil and let her put a flat hand in the gap.
  7. Leave him up. He comes off the hall wall on Thursday morning and goes back up flat on the exhibition wall, and everything made this week joins him there.

💡Let her name him something daft and write it as she says it. A dinosaur called Baby Sandwich gets talked about for weeks.

Day 303 · For the grown-up The Dinosaur on the Hall Wall · Saturday, October 30
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and will walk the whole stretch on his own feet if nobody hurries him. Hand him the loose end of the string and ask him to carry it to the chalk cross. He will drop it halfway and want it back. Count his paces beside Azlyn's so he gets the rhythm long before the numbers.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Kreston has ten or more words at 16 months, and a shape that size on the wall pulls most of them out of him. Hold him up to touch the nose and name it. He will point at it every time you carry him past for the rest of the month. At the farm keep him on your hip at the fences and let him do the pointing.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Making the edges teaches shapes faster than naming them.

You could hold up a picture and name the parts, and some of it would stick. Tracing an outline with her own finger puts the shape through her hands, and hands are where a three-year-old files this sort of thing. Studies comparing children who look at a shape with children who trace it find the tracers pick that shape out later in new sizes and colors. An edge is the whole of what makes a shape a shape, and one slow trip round it carries more than the word dinosaur does. She cut none of it and she owns the outline.

⚠️

Safety: The craft knife is adult only, it cuts flattened cardboard on the floor, and it goes back out of reach every time you stop. A six-foot sheet of card propped against a wall can come down on a 16-month-old, so the dinosaur goes up taped flat and stays taped flat. Measuring runs on the sidewalk, so lay the string on the house side of the walk, keep Kreston on your hand the whole stretch, and stop at every driveway to look.

Trying the Tail On

You need: the old hooded top · 1 old sock · 2 safety pins.

  1. Pin the empty sock to the back hem of the top and let her put the whole thing on.
  2. Send her down the hall, onto a chair and up two stairs in it. A tail that catches on a stair gets shortened now.
  3. Ask where the spikes start and where they stop. She marks both places with a finger, and six arrive at 9:15.

The Dinosaur Suit

⏱️ 60 min🧰 9 items

You need: 1 old hooded top or sweatshirt, Thick card, 6 sheets, or 3 cereal boxes, Masking tape and packing tape, Newspaper, a stack, 1 old sock, or a leg cut from old tights, 4 safety pins, Kitchen foil, for the strips that catch a headlight, 1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), Poster paint and 1 brush, or 2 thick markers

  1. Cut six triangles from the card with the adult scissors, biggest to smallest. She lines them up in order while you cut.
  2. She paints them, or fills them in with the markers. Thick and fast, and they dry while you build the tail.
  3. Stuff the sock with scrunched newspaper until it holds a curve, then shut the end with packing tape.
  4. Lay the top face down. Masking-tape the triangles along the spine, points up, with a strip over every base, then tape a band of foil down the tail and another across the front so a headlight picks her up tonight.
  5. Pin the tail through the hem with the four safety pins, low enough to swing and short enough to stay off her heels.
  6. She puts it on and walks the hall. Whatever falls off now gets more tape.

💡Tape the spikes and pin the tail. Both come off in a minute at bedtime.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Walking the Route in Daylight

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk tonight's route now, in the light, with the suit on. Count the houses you will knock at, let her choose which, and name the last one out loud. Wet sidewalk under a streetlight is slick, so find the bad patches while you can see them.

Six Colors, Two Lights

Pick a room with curtains that shut and gut the pumpkin in it.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 9 items

You need: 6 objects in strong flat colors from round the house, 1 flashlight with fresh batteries, 1 battery tealight, 1 small pumpkin, 1 large metal spoon, 1 sharp knife (adult only), 1 orange or red candy wrapper, or a piece of colored cellophane, Paper and 1 marker, A room with curtains that shut

  1. She picks six things in six strong colors and lines them up in daylight. Write the names down as she says them.
  2. Cut the lid off the pumpkin with the sharp knife while she stands back, then hand her the metal spoon and let her scrape it hollow.
  3. She points at where the eyes and the mouth go. You cut them, big and simple, while she stands back.
  4. Shut the curtains. Go along the row with the flashlight and ask which ones changed. Write her answers under the first list.
  5. Drop the battery tealight into the pumpkin, turn the flashlight off and look again. The reds hold their ground and the blues go gray.
  6. Hold the candy wrapper over the flashlight and light the row through it. The red thing vanishes and she will say so before you do.
  7. Big light back on, and read her both lists.

💡Do this before the trick-or-treating. By six she will be too wound up to notice a color changing.

Day 304 · For the grown-up Halloween After Dark · Sunday, October 31
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and would rather walk this than ride it. Take the stroller anyway and let him out for the last stretch. He copies chores now, so give him the empty candy bag to carry to the gate.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Kreston is 16 months and copies whatever your hands are doing, so give him a bowl of the scooped pumpkin flesh at the table beside her. Nothing sharp goes near him. He will not last the evening, so take him to four houses in the carrier and bring him home.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Light changes what she thinks a color is.

Azlyn has spent a year learning that a thing has a color, and this afternoon she found out the color depends on what is shining on it. You hold a red coat as red under a streetlight without noticing the work, a trick called color constancy that takes years to firm up, so a changed color lands harder on her than on you. Flashlight and a tealight carry different amounts of red and blue, and a blue object under a warm light has nothing to give back. Her two lists stay on the table where she can go back and check them.

⚠️

Safety: A sharp knife going into a hard pumpkin is adult work, and wet pumpkin on a hard floor is as slippery as ice, so wipe it up as you go. No real candle goes inside a lit pumpkin with Kreston walking. The tail stays short enough not to trip her and never loops round a neck. Tonight is the one evening of the year when small children are out on residential roads in the dark, so the suit carries its foil strips down the tail and across the front, she carries one flashlight in her outside hand, and her other hand is in yours at every driveway and every curb. Cross beside her rather than behind her, walk the sidewalk side of every parked car, and keep her off the road side of you the whole way. Kreston rides in the stroller or the carrier from the front door to the front door. Pumpkin seeds and Halloween candy are both choking size at 16 months, so the seed bowl stays up on the counter, the bag gets sorted with him in the high chair and then goes onto a high shelf, and the floor is swept before he is down. The scissors stay with you.

The Color With Her Name On It

You need: red and yellow food coloring · 1 shallow bowl · 1 teaspoon · masking tape and a marker.

  1. Half a cup of water in the shallow bowl. Two drops of yellow, then red one drop at a time, stirred with the teaspoon, until she says stop.
  2. Ask what that color is called. Write whatever comes out of her mouth on masking tape stuck to the bowl.
  3. Tell her every flower today comes out of this bowl, so her name goes on all of them.

Marigolds From Paper Towels

⏱️ 60 min🧰 8 items

You need: Paper towels, 1 roll, Her mixed orange in the shallow bowl, topped up with water, 2 baking trays for drying, Drinking straws or garden twigs, 12, Masking tape, 6 clothespins, 1 jam jar, Newspaper, for the table and for drying

  1. Newspaper over the table. Tear the roll into squares, about sixty, and stack them beside the bowl.
  2. She dips a square corner first and lays it flat on the newspaper. Wet paper tears under a hand, so three at a time and no more.
  3. Carry them through to newspaper spread along the radiator, the two trays under the wettest of them. Half an hour to go stiff, and they darken as they dry.
  4. Gather three dry squares at the middle, scrunch, and bind the gather to a straw with masking tape. That is one marigold.
  5. Twelve of them, and she takes over the scrunching after two. Clip the two dozen spare squares into a bundle so they stop blowing about.
  6. Stand the whole dozen in the jam jar in the middle of the table.

💡The color dries three shades darker than it looks wet. Say so before she puts more red in to fix it.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Orange Hunt Down the Street

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

The first of November, and your street is as orange as it gets all year. Walk out with an old envelope and collect whatever matches the bowl: a beech leaf, a curl of orange peel, a chip of brick, half a bus ticket. Hold each one against the sky, then against the sidewalk; the same leaf passes one test and fails the other. She turns down half of what she picks up.

The Path of Petals to the Table

Today is Día de los Muertos, when families in Mexico set a table for the people they have lost and lay a path of marigold petals so the dead can find their way to it. The table gets set for the people who are not coming, and she lays the path to it.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 8 items

You need: The jar of marigolds from this morning, and the bundle of spare dyed squares, A low table or the coffee table, cleared bare, 3–6 printed photographs, or your phone propped up, 2 battery tealights, 1 small plate per person, Paper and crayons, Masking tape, 1 pitcher of water

  1. Clear the low table to bare wood. Nothing with a corner Kreston can get a hand round.
  2. She tears a dozen of the spare squares into petals and lays a path from the front door to the table, taping down the ones that curl.
  3. Stand the photographs along the back edge, or prop your phone up with the pictures running.
  4. The jar of marigolds goes in the middle, a battery tealight either side.
  5. Everybody names one person and one food that person liked. A small plate of it comes out for each name, and she carries them all.
  6. Paper and crayons, and one card for the dinosaurs, who are also gone and still get named in this house.
  7. Stand the pitcher of water on the table; the tradition says the ones who come back arrive thirsty. Say all the names before dinner.

💡Let her set it in her own order. A plate of fries beside a photograph of a great-grandmother is right, and tidying it makes her table yours.

Day 305 · For the grown-up Día de los Muertos and the Marigold Path · Monday, November 1
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and points at everything he has a word for, so hand the spotting to him. Walk slower than you want and wait him out. He passes you leaves you had stepped over and names most of them.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Kreston is 16 months and pulls on anything with an edge, so nothing on the low table hangs over the side while he is loose. Give him the last of the dyed squares to tear at your feet, a job that holds him for five or ten minutes at a time, and he comes back to it twice. Out on the grass he chases the ball further than he kicks it.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Naming a color she invented does more than learning the standard eleven.

English hands Azlyn eleven basic color words. Other languages cut the same spectrum up in other places: Russian keeps two separate words where English has blue, and some languages get by on five terms in total. The lines between colors are a convention she is taught, so a child who mixes a shade and names it herself finds out those lines are not fixed. Her word for what came out of that bowl will be gone by spring. The discovery under it, that color names are ours to move, will outlast it by years. People made the names up, and this morning she found out she is allowed to make one.

⚠️

Safety: A real candle on a low table sits inside a 16-month-old's reach, and so do glass frames and a cloth he can haul down on himself. Use battery tealights, keep cloth and overhang off the tabletop, stand the jar in the middle out of his pulling reach, and put out copies or phone photographs rather than the framed originals. Torn paper towels go into Kreston's mouth and neat food coloring stains everything on the way through, so he tears his squares where you can see him and the scraps get swept up before you sit down.

The Bones Under the Oats

You need: the oat tray with the bones buried · 1 large spoon · 1 pastry brush.

  1. She digs with the spoon until she turns up the first one, then swaps to the brush, which slows the finding down.
  2. Every bone she lifts out goes on the table in a line, notches showing.
  3. She counts what she has. Tell her how many are still under the oats, and she keeps going until the tray is empty.

🎨 MAKE
The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Slot That Only Fits One Way

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: 12–15 cardboard bone shapes cut from 2 large boxes the night before, two or three notches in each, every notch an inch and a half deep and the width of the card, 1 permanent marker, Dry oats or rice, 5 cups (500 g), in a deep tray, 1 large spoon and 1 clean pastry brush or old toothbrush, Masking tape for repairs

  1. Lay every bone out with its notches showing. Number the two biggest 1 and 2 in permanent marker, because the rest hangs off those.
  2. Show her one join and stop talking. Two notches face each other, slide together, and the pieces stand at a right angle.
  3. She works out the rest by turning. A piece that will not go is upside down or back to front, so hand it back rather than flipping it.
  4. Torn corners get masking tape, and a notch that has gone slack gets a strip across it. By the end the skeleton stands on the table with nothing holding it.
  5. Photograph it standing, then bury two pieces back in the oats and let her hunt them out with the spoon and the brush while you clear up.

💡Turning a piece round for her hands her the answer. She will take four times as long over it as you would.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

Her Print Beside the Big One

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Take the chalk to the flattest sidewalk you have and draw one enormous three- toed print, the size of a trash can lid. She stands in the middle of it while you chalk round both her rain boots. She will want to know whether all of her fits inside the big foot, so let her lie down in it. Chalk will not take on damp November stone, so pick a dry patch under a wall.

Second main event · 1:00–2:30 PM

The Footprints He Left Behind

Twenty prints cut from junk mail, and she decides where every one of them lands.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 6 items

You need: Junk mail, catalogs or cereal-box card, 20 sheets, 1 permanent marker, 1 pair of child-safe scissors for her, 1 pair of adult scissors for you, 1 roll low-tack masking tape, 1 tape measure, 1 stick of chalk

  1. Draw a fat three-toed print on the first sheet of junk mail in marker and cut it out with the adult scissors. That one is the template.
  2. Draw round it on the other nineteen. She cuts the easy ones with the child-safe scissors while you do the fiddly ones.
  3. Number them 1 to 20 in marker as they come off the pile.
  4. She lays the trail from the front door to the standing skeleton, in her order, and you come behind pressing every tape edge flat.
  5. Walk the trail together, counting out loud, one number to a print.
  6. Run the tape measure from the first print to the last and read her the number. Chalk it on the doorstep so she can show somebody.
  7. Leave the trail down. Thursday's visitors walk it.

💡Use low-tack tape or you peel the wall. Test a piece on the baseboard and leave it ten minutes before you trust it.

  • Run the trail up the stairs and nowhere else.

Day 306 · For the grown-up Bones That Fit Together · Tuesday, November 2
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and follows a line on the ground now the way older children follow a curb. Chalk him a short trail of small prints from the gate to the big one and walk it holding one of his hands. He copies everything, so keep a fat sidewalk chalk in your hand with his hand over the top of it.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Kreston swims too. At 16 months he will walk down the shallow steps holding the rail rather than be carried, so let him, with a hand on him throughout. Twenty minutes and out. Back home he will peel a paper print off the floor and bring it to you.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Fitting a shape into a hole is a test of mental rotation.

Azlyn turning a notched piece over and over is running the calculation with her arms, because she cannot yet run it behind her eyes. You picture the rotation in your head and then move once. She moves first and checks, and the checking is how the picturing gets built. Studies that give young children puzzles and blocks find the ones who handle more of them do better on spatial tasks years later, and the handling is the active ingredient. Every piece she picks up the wrong way round is one more repetition, so leave the hour clear, keep your hands off the pile, and let her come back to it in bursts.

⚠️

Safety: An open tray of dry oats is an inhalation and a choking risk for Kreston at 16 months, so it comes up off the floor the moment he is loose. All the notch cutting happens the night before, out of reach of both of them, and the craft knife does not come out again today. A stub of chalk is choking size at his age, so he gets a fat one, in your hand, and it comes back to you when you stand up. Paper taped to a hard floor slides underfoot, so press every edge flat. The big print goes on a stretch of sidewalk with no driveway crossing it, and both children stay on the house side of the walk. The adult scissors stay with you. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

The Line From Lightest to Darkest

You need: 10 green patches torn from the magazine stack · a clear bit of table.

  1. Tear ten greens out of the pile, all of them different, and drop them in front of her in a heap.
  2. She lays them in a line from palest to darkest. The two she cannot decide between stay where she puts them.
  3. Ask which one is leaf green and which one is dinosaur green. Take both answers and leave the line out until 9:15.

The main event · 9:15–10:15 AM

The Skin Made of Torn Paper

⏱️ 60 min🧰 6 items

You need: Junk mail, catalogs and magazines, a stack, 2 glue sticks, or a bowl of flour-and-water paste, The cardboard dinosaur from Saturday, or one drawn on a flattened box in ten minutes, 1 permanent marker, 1 shallow tray, or 3 plates, for sorting the torn pieces, 1 damp cloth

  1. Take the dinosaur off the wall and lay him flat. Draw one marker line down his length: light side below it, dark side above.
  2. Three plates, or three corners of the tray: dark greens, pale greens, browns. She tears the junk mail up and sorts for twenty minutes before any glue comes out.
  3. Glue stick onto the card, pieces pressed down overlapping, palest along the belly and darkest along the spine.
  4. She will lay two greens side by side that fight each other. Leave them. Ask her at the end which pair she would swap.
  5. Browns fill the gaps. Keep the damp cloth going on her fingers.
  6. Put him back on the wall while he is still wet and let him dry up there.

💡Torn edges beat cut ones today. A tear shows the white core of the paper, and the pieces read as scales.

🌳 OUTSIDE
Get outside · 10:30–11:15 AM

The Last Green Leaves

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Early November has taken most of the green off the trees, so today it is a hunt. Ivy on a wall, a holly, a laurel hedge, moss along a north-facing curb, grass still growing. Bring one of each home, five greens in a bag, and hold them against the dinosaur in the hall.

The Labels She Dictates

Tomorrow the week goes on show. Today she names each thing and you write it down.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: Cereal-box card and paper, 10 sheets, 1 permanent marker and crayons, 1 pair of child-safe scissors, Masking tape, 6 feet of string and 6 clothespins, 1 pencil, Everything made this week, gathered onto one table

  1. Gather the week onto one table: the lamps, the marigolds, the suit, the skeleton, one spare footprint. The dinosaur stays on the wall.
  2. Point at each thing and ask what it is. Write her answer on a card in marker, word for word, wrong grammar left in.
  3. She decorates every card in crayon and cuts it out with the child-safe scissors, however wonky.
  4. Pencil the weekday on the back of each card so tomorrow's sorting is quick.
  5. Six tickets on paper, one per visitor, and she draws on all of them.
  6. Clip the cards along the string between two chair backs so she can see the whole week hanging in a row, then take the string down and put it away.
  7. Tape one card to the front door saying what tomorrow is. She dictates that one too.

💡Write what she says and nothing else. The one what I made with the spikey is the funniest thing in the house tomorrow.

Day 307 · For the grown-up The Right Kind of Green · Wednesday, November 3
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so give him the bag and let him hold it open at every stop. He will try to eat a leaf, so the ivy and the holly ride home in your pocket. He has a word for tree now and uses it on everything with a trunk.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Kreston is 16 months and cannot be trusted near the exhibition table, so set him up at the far end with his own paper and a crayon. He scribbles with a fist grip and fills a page. Give him a card with his name on it, because he goes in the exhibition too. At the play center, twenty minutes in the under-twos part.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Matching a shade is much harder than matching a color.

Azlyn has green nailed and stalls on which green. The word covers a wide band, and telling two of them apart means holding one in her head while she looks at the other, which loads her memory rather than her eyes. Children sort by color category long before they can rank shades, and the ranking turns up around four or five. Laying ten scraps out from pale to dark this morning was hard work, and the two she could not place were the two she was working hardest on. Expect her line to be right at both ends and muddled in the middle.

⚠️

Safety: A string clipped between two chair backs sits at her chest height, which is his neck height, so it comes down the moment she has looked at the row. Ivy and holly are both poisonous, and Kreston still puts leaves in his mouth at 16 months, so those two travel home in your pocket.

The Last Piece

You need: whatever is still unfinished · crayons or paint.

  1. Walk the house together and find the one thing from this week nobody finished: a lamp with a bare patch, a card with no name, a footprint still on the pile.
  2. She finishes it at the table on her own while you drink your tea and stay out of it.

Everything in the Order She Picks

⏱️ 60 min🧰 5 items

You need: Everything made this week: the dinosaur, the slot skeleton, the lamps, the marigolds, the footprints, Masking tape, including the low-tack roll for the floor line, 1 dining chair for the ticket desk, Yesterday's labels, 1 permanent marker and spare card

  1. Carry the whole week to the wall in one go and leave it in a heap on the floor. Let her stand and look at the heap.
  2. She places them, one at a time, in her order. You carry whatever is too heavy and say nothing about grouping them by size or by day.
  3. Every piece gets yesterday's label taped beside it, at her height rather than yours.
  4. Anything with no label gets one now, in marker on spare card, dictated the same way as the others.
  5. Run a strip of low-tack masking tape along the floor to mark the line visitors stay behind, and set the chair at the end as the ticket desk.
  6. Walk it yourself as a visitor while she watches, and ask her one question at every stop.

💡Her order will not be yours. The lamps next to the footprints because they are both little is a reason, and it is hers.

Delivering the First Invitation

⏱️ 45 min🌳 outdoors

Walk the first invitation round to a neighbor who might come this afternoon. She carries it the whole way, knocks, and hands it over on the doorstep, or posts it through the mail slot if nobody answers. The light goes before six now, so take the long way round and use the daylight while it is there.

Doors Open at One

She ran a carnival gate back in August and sold tickets at it. Today the tickets are free, the visitors keep their hands behind the line, and the whole thing runs on her telling them what each thing is.

⏱️ 90 min🧰 7 items

You need: The laid-out exhibition, Her ticket cards from yesterday, Your phone, for filming and for calling Grandma, The party tea on a tray, 1 flashlight, 1 chair for every person who comes, The labels

  1. She hands a ticket to everybody in the house, Kreston included.
  2. Doors open at one. She walks the group along the exhibition in her own order and says what each thing is. Read the label out after she has spoken, never before.
  3. Film it on your phone held low, so you get her hands and the objects with her voice over the top.
  4. Turn the big light off at one exhibit and let her light it with the flashlight. She picks which one.
  5. Call Grandma and carry the phone round the whole wall again, at her pace, so she gets to do the tour twice.
  6. Peel the tape line off the floor. Put a chair out for each person, and the party tea on the floor in the middle.
  7. Everybody says which thing was their favorite and why. She goes last.

💡Let her run it. She will muddle the order, miss two things out and double back for them. Nobody corrects her in front of an audience.

Day 308 · For the grown-up Opening Day · Thursday, November 4
👶 Infant integration morning

Kreston is 16 months and posts things through any gap he can find. Write a second envelope and let him push it through the flap with your hand under his. Expect to lift him back up to that mail slot twice more before he will leave it.

👶 Kreston's afternoon 1:00 onward

Kreston is 16 months and gets a ticket like everybody else. He walks the tour holding a hand and reaches for whatever he should not, so move the fragile end of the wall out of range before one o'clock. He has ten or more words and he will spend one of them on the dinosaur. That is the bit of the movie you keep.

🧠 One thing worth knowing

Finishing something that took all week is its own lesson.

Azlyn lives in single afternoons, so a week is a long stretch to hold one thing across, and she held it. Monday's marigolds were still on the table on Thursday and she can see how they got there. Work that runs over days asks a three-year-old to remember a plan, come back to something half done, and wait for the payoff, three separate skills that arrive with practice and not otherwise. Standing in front of a wall she filled and telling somebody what is on it shuts the loop she opened last Friday. She will ask for another one, and that is worth a yes.

⚠️

Safety: The visitor line is tape on the floor rather than string, because a line at her chest height is at his neck height. The standing cardboard dinosaur stays taped flat to the wall or laid down on the floor while Kreston is loose in the room.
